title: Getting Less Wrong Without Becoming Certain
summary: Reading Yudkowsky's Sequences alongside Hume, with Bayesian updating, human utility functions, model uncertainty and the premises behind Roko's basilisk.
text: 8 November 2026 · Philosophy & inference · 13 min read Getting Less Wrong Without Becoming Certain Updated 11 November 2026 The most useful question in Eliezer Yudkowsky’s Sequences is what would make you change your mind. It is easy to admire that question and much harder to give an answer that puts a cherished belief at risk. Written between 2006 and 2009, these linked essays helped establish the intellectual vocabulary of LessWrong, a community site about reasoning, decision-making and AI. They are informal, argumentative and often enjoyable. They also range from practical advice about belief revision to much larger claims about morality and intelligence. Those claims deserve separate consideration. Reading the essays does not require adopting the whole package. [ 1 ] What interests me is the boundary between improving a model and justifying the assumptions behind it. Hume is a useful companion here, but treating him as someone the Sequences simply forgot would miss much of what they actually say. The useful part is a habit of checking Yudkowsky separates epistemic rationality, improving beliefs, from instrumental rationality, achieving what is valued. The map–territory distinction keeps a description of the world separate from the world itself. His definition explicitly allows uncertainty. Criticizing it for promising direct, infallible access to reality would target a position it rejects. [ 2 ] Making Beliefs Pay Rent asks what observations a belief leads you to expect. A scientific-sounding explanation that accommodates every possible outcome has given up an important way to be corrected. This advice is particularly useful when a technical discussion becomes a competition over who knows the right terminology. [ 3 ] That habit also needs to turn inward. Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People describes how knowledge of cognitive errors can become ammunition against other people while leaving one’s own beliefs untouched. It is one of the strongest essays in the collection because it identifies a failure its own readers are especially well equipped to rationalize. [ 4 ] Hume leaves room for better predictions Hume’s problem of induction concerns the move from observed cases to unobserved ones. Past regularity cannot deductively establish that the next case will follow the same pattern. Defending that inference by pointing to induction’s past success uses the very inference under examination. [ 5 ] The claim that a 99% probability is no closer to knowledge than a 1% probability therefore goes too far. Neither guarantees truth. They nevertheless make very different predictions, support different decisions and can perform very differently against observations. Denying certainty does not erase those distinctions. Nor does being a situated observer make public comparison impossible. An agreed measurement procedure can expose a disagreement without providing a view from nowhere. The Sequences’ rejection of absolute confidence is explicit in 0 And 1 Are Not Probabilities . Its practical point is that assigning zero prior probability prevents ordinary Bayesian updating from recovering a possibility. The title should not be mistaken for a prohibition in probability theory, where zero and one are legitimate probabilities. [ 6 ] Hume’s own sceptical solution turns toward the habits by which experience guides expectation. It offers no instruction to stop reasoning. A productive disagreement concerns how much justification prediction supplies, rather than whether fallible creatures are permitted to predict at all. [ 7 ] Bayes updates a model with assumptions For a hypothesis \(H\), evidence \(E\) and a model \(M\), Bayesian updating gives $$P(H\mid E,M)=\frac{P(E\mid H,M)P(H\mid M)}{P(E\mid M)}.$$ The explicit \(M\) matters. The posterior distribution depends on the hypotheses considered, their priors and the likelihood assigned to the observations. Bayesian updating does not add hypotheses missing from the model or establish whether a measurement procedure transfers to a new setting. Consider an invented defect test with 90% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate. With a 1% defect prior, one positive result raises the defect probability to about 15.4%. If test outcomes are independent conditional on defect status, two positive results raise it to about 76.6%. Reading the same positive report twice supplies only one observation. Multiplying its likelihood ratio twice would overstate the evidence. How much evidence is actually new? A constructed example with a fixed test, not measured manufacturing data. Prior defect probability 1% Positive reports 2 Independent tests 76.6% Copies of one report 15.4% The first row assumes independent test outcomes conditional on whether the defect exists. The second repeats the same information. Sensitivity is 90%; the false-positive rate is 5%. At the defaults, two independent positive tests give 76.6%; two copies of one positive report give 15.4%. This is a practical weakness of long speculative arguments. Several apparently independent reasons may descend from one source or share the same untested assumption. A precise final number can hide uncertainty about the structure that produced it. Priors need not be arbitrary, but giving a prior a decimal expansion does not make its justification stronger. Gelman and Shalizi’s account of Bayesian practice emphasizes model checking and revision alongside fitting. A useful test asks where observations disagree with data generated by the fitted model. Such discrepancies can reveal a need for new hypotheses, new measurements or a different likelihood. [ 8 ] Getting less wrong can consequently mean better calibration, better discrimination between cases, fewer failed predictions or improved decisions on fresh data. None requires certainty. The evidential case becomes weaker when feedback is distant, outcomes are poorly defined or the model can explain away every failure. That limitation applies to any forecasting culture, including one fluent in Bayesian language. A utility function needs an ethical argument Bayesian decision theory adds preferences to beliefs. In a simplified finite setting, the selected action maximizes expected utility over possible states, $$a^*=\arg\max_a\sum_s P(s\mid E,M)\,U(a,s).$$ The probabilities describe uncertainty; \(U\) assigns value to the consequences. Decision theory can expose an inconsistency in a set of preferences or show which action follows from them. The formalism does not, by itself, establish whose preferences deserve authority. Expected-utility maximization is also broader than ethical utilitarianism. Its utility function can represent many kinds of concern, rather than only a sum of happiness. [ 9 ] Hume’s is–ought passage asks for an explanation when an argument moves from descriptions to prescriptions. In the equation, much of that work enters through \(U\). Facts about what people presently want do not automatically settle what should be protected, which desires are distorted by coercion or how conflicts should be resolved. Naming the utility function makes those choices visible; it does not finish the ethical argument. [ 10 ] Yudkowsky does engage with metaethics. Setting Up Metaethics examines the attraction and difficulties of morality as something given and morality as preference. No Universally Compelling Arguments rejects the expectation that an argument must persuade every possible mind. Neither text supports the simple picture of a cosmic moral theorem that any sufficiently clever machine inevitably discovers. [ 11 , 12 ] It would be equally misleading to summarize his position as whatever anyone happens to want. Morality as Fixed Computation discusses an optimizer that changes a person’s desires to make them easier to satisfy. The essay rejects that as a faithful realization of what people value. His naturalistic account tries to preserve the content of moral judgment, including the possibility of moral error. Whether it succeeds is a philosophical question beyond the decision rule. [ 13 ] Whose values survive reflection? Fun Theory is more interesting than its name suggests. It explores why pleasure alone may leave out challenge, agency, relationships and the experience of doing something oneself. It treats a desirable future as a demanding design problem. This is a substantial corrective to the idea that rationalist ethics consists of maximizing a single obvious number. [ 14 ] Yudkowsky’s earlier proposal of coherent extrapolated volition asks, roughly, what people would want with greater understanding and reflection, then seeks a coherent collective direction. It is an attempt to avoid encoding the immediate wishes of a programmer as humanity’s destination. Its open problem is how to define and carry out that extrapolation. [ 15 ] The unresolved choices are consequential. Who is represented? Which changes count as learning and which as manipulation? What happens when informed people continue to disagree? A model of human preferences can help investigate these questions, but its designer still chooses the conditions under which those preferences are elicited and revised. Aggregation adds another choice. Suppose a social objective is \(U_{\mathrm{social}}=\sum_i w_i U_i\). Selecting the weights and making utilities comparable across people requires justification. For an individual, replacing \(U_i\) with \(c_iU_i+d_i\), where \(c_i>0\), preserves their expected-utility ranking. In a sum across people, changing one person’s scale can change the collective decision unless the weights compensate. The arithmetic cannot choose the interpersonal scale for us. A utility monster pushes on that aggregation problem. A hypothetical being that obtains vastly more benefit from resources would dominate a particular additive rule. Whether that is acceptable depends on the rule’s ethical justification, the interests represented and any protections it includes. Greater intelligence or power does not itself make the being’s preferences morally authoritative. The same question remains if it can rewrite everyone else’s preferences. The basilisk depends on much more than a large number Roko’s basilisk is a 2010 thought experiment associated with LessWrong, not a summary of the Sequences or a doctrine generally accepted by the site. Rob Bensinger’s retrospective explicitly distinguishes the original argument from the mythology around it. It is a poor basis for diagnosing an entire community. [ 16 ] In its familiar form, a future AI threatens to punish simulated versions of people who knew about it but did not help bring it into existence. The proposed incentive relies on present decisions being linked to a future policy, despite the future system having no ordinary causal route into the past. It also needs assumptions about prediction, credible commitments, the moral status of simulations and why a present person should treat a future copy’s suffering as a threat to themselves. These premises do the work. Ordinary expected-utility maximization alone does not entail the threat. If punishment is costly and cannot alter any earlier action, carrying it out has no obvious benefit. A different decision theory or commitment mechanism would have to explain why the policy is adopted and why the present agent responds. Adding enjoyment of torture changes the objective again; it cannot serve as an explanation of what a benevolent optimizer must do. The resemblance to Pascal’s wager lies in enormous stakes attached to a speculative story. LessWrong’s own discussion of Pascal’s mugging examines how very large utilities can overwhelm small probabilities. Rejecting every low-probability concern would be reckless, but multiplying an unsupported story by an enormous payoff does not improve the evidence for the story. Competing threats and alternative uses of the same resources also belong in the comparison. [ 17 ] The ethical concern is still worth keeping. An additive objective may permit serious harm to a minority for a sufficiently large benefit elsewhere. Anyone endorsing that objective owes an account of those trade-offs. The basilisk’s peculiar account of incentives is a separate argument, and a useful criticism has to say which premise it rejects. Taking AI risk seriously without treating a forecast as destiny The AI argument associated with this writing has a defensible core. Competence does not automatically imply benevolence, and a system may pursue a poorly specified objective in ways its designers did not intend. The orthogonality thesis concerns possible combinations of capability and goals; it does not predict which combinations a particular training process will produce. [ 18 ] The safety argument becomes more informative when its steps are examined separately. A physical basis for human intelligence leaves the engineering timeline open. Faster computation must still translate into usable competence, access to resources and influence over the world. Risk estimates depend on the evidence for each link and on how failures or successes at one stage affect the next. Future people can matter morally without every forecast about their lives being reliable. A decision about resources combines a model of what an intervention can change with a judgment about the value of those changes. Uncertainty in both deserves attention. Useful responses include work that helps across several plausible futures, tests that can expose mistaken assumptions and opportunities to revise decisions as evidence arrives. Read the essays, then give the claims something to answer to I recommend the Sequences as an approachable collection of ideas to argue with. Making Beliefs Pay Rent , Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People and the opening distinctions in What Do We Mean By Rationality? are good places to begin. Fun Theory and the metaethics essays give a much fairer view of the moral project than the basilisk story does. My reservation concerns the step from disciplined reasoning to confidence in a comprehensive worldview. A coherent argument can retain shared errors throughout its chain. Technical language can make an untested assumption harder to notice. These are risks of any ambitious philosophy, and the collection contains resources for criticizing them. Science Doesn’t Trust Your Rationality emphasizes procedures that can correct a reasoner who does not notice their own mistakes. [ 19 ] Hume keeps the foundations open to examination. Bayesian methods make beliefs and decisions more explicit. Experiments, historical evidence, other people’s experience and ethical argument constrain different parts of the resulting picture. Posterior claims should state the priors, likelihoods and model assumptions they depend on. Ethical recommendations should state the values they use. Which observation would change the forecast? Which assumption changes the recommended action? Whose interests were left out of the objective? Getting less wrong is valuable when answering those questions changes what happens next. title: Text to Trajectory
summary: How grounding, task programs, motion planning and learned robot policies turn language into movement, with a focused evaluation proposed for Visual Components.
text: 1 November 2026 · Robotics & language · 12 min read Text to Trajectory Updated 11 November 2026 “Place the red carrier to the right of the blue carrier, passing over the marker.” A robot can reach the correct destination without a collision and still fail that instruction. The route matters as much as the endpoint. An industrial controller needs object identities, coordinates, actions and limits. The sentence supplies some of those indirectly and leaves others unstated. Turning it into motion brings language grounding, program generation, planning and control into the same system. This review follows the interfaces between them, with Visual Components as a possible simulation backend. A route is part of the request The carrier example contains an object to move, a reference object, a spatial relation and a route requirement. “Right” also needs a coordinate frame. A gap needs units and a tolerance. “Do that again” needs a record of the last successful task and a decision about which parts should be recomputed after the scene changes. A structured description makes these choices inspectable. Early Generalized Grounding Graphs connect language to candidate objects, places, paths and events, preserving more of the command than an object label alone. Their central problem remains current even when a neural model performs the translation. [ 1 ] A task can be perfectly valid under its encoded rules while missing a requirement from the sentence. If “over the marker” disappears during translation, a downstream solver has no reason to include it. Checking meaning therefore needs access to the original request, rather than only to the generated program. Grounding the scene CLIP learns visual and textual features that make matching image–text pairs similar. This gives a perception system a useful way to search by description. Precise manipulation also needs spatial information about where an object is and how the robot can interact with it. [ 2 ] CLIPort combines CLIP-based semantic features with a spatial pathway for pick-and-place prediction. The two streams help distinguish what to manipulate and where to act. The resulting affordance maps belong to a learned manipulation policy; a separate industrial planner may instead need an object identifier, a pose and explicit geometric constraints. [ 3 ] Figure 1. CLIPort combines semantic features with spatial precision for manipulation. Reproduced from Shridhar, 2021 . Open full-size figure . Persistent scene representations help when a task extends beyond one camera image. SayPlan searches a hierarchical 3D scene graph for relevant objects and places, then combines language planning with classical path planning and simulator feedback. Collapsing irrelevant parts of the graph reduces the information the language model has to process. [ 4 ] Figure 2. SayPlan exposes a compact part of a larger scene and uses execution-related feedback to revise its plan. Reproduced from Rana, 2023 . Open full-size figure . Work on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) studies when separately trained modalities learn matching representations. Its alignment theorem assumes matched views of the same underlying states and additional idealisations. Object references and route requirements need a further task-level test, because a rotation between aligned feature spaces does not specify either one. [ 5 ] Turning a request into callable work SayCan chooses among available skills using both language relevance and an estimate of whether a skill can succeed. Code as Policies gives generated programs more freedom to process perception, calculate geometric quantities and call control APIs. The choice changes what must be checked. Selecting a known skill requires reliable preconditions; generated code also introduces arguments, control flow and assumptions that can be wrong. [ 6 , 7 ] NeSyRo checks generated policy code symbolically and gathers further observations when the available state is insufficient. That separates some code errors from missing knowledge about the scene. The checks remain limited by the properties represented in the symbolic model. [ 8 ] Industrial integration makes the interface concrete. Syniawa and colleagues use AutomationML state descriptions and a defined skill library, translating instructions into process steps and C++ calls in simulated cabinet assembly with ROS 2 and MoveIt 2. A Visual Components implementation would need an equally explicit account of scene objects, callable skills and their inputs. The simulator name alone says little about that contract. [ 9 ] Making the movement feasible Task-and-motion planning connects discrete choices with continuous geometry. A requested placement may require a different grasp, a different action order or moving an obstruction first. A collision report is useful to the task planner only if it can revise one of those choices in response. [ 10 ] VoxPoser translates language and visual detections into 3D preference and constraint maps that a motion planner can optimize. ReKep uses relationships between visual keypoints, expressed as functions over task stages and transitions. Both give the requested behavior a spatial representation that reaches beyond a named final pose. [ 11 , 12 ] Figure 3. ReKep distinguishes subgoal constraints from constraints on the movement between subgoals. Reproduced from Huang, 2024 . Open full-size figure . For the red carrier, a final right-of relation constrains placement. Passing over the marker constrains the carried object during transport. Checking only the gripper endpoint would leave the route untested. Even a correct route description can be infeasible with the current grasp, obstacle layout or joint limits. A collision-free geometric path also has to be timed and tracked. cuRobo uses GPU-parallel inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization to search efficiently. cuRoboV2 adds dynamics-aware B-spline optimization with torque limits and depth-derived obstacle distance fields. These methods improve the motion computation once the goal and constraints have been supplied. [ 13 , 14 ] Figure 4. cuRoboV2 includes motion constraints that a geometric path alone does not capture. Reproduced from Sundaralingam, 2026 . Open full-size figure . The remaining assumptions matter at execution. Payload, collision geometry, contact behavior, attachment state and controller tracking determine which motions the model represents accurately. A simulator can check its own model precisely while omitting a physical effect that matters on the real cell. Smaller models with stronger checks A restricted industrial vocabulary can make compact task models practical. Ro-SLM distils instruction and operation-code knowledge into smaller models. Its 8B configuration reports 97.7% success on simple UAV tasks and 70% on complex ones. The difference between those settings is more informative than a single claim that a small model works. [ 15 ] SLoSa constructs safety-aware examples with classical planners, a teacher model and formal verifiers, then combines supervised adaptation with verification-guided reinforcement learning. It evaluates formal domains, household simulators, edge hardware and a desktop arm. Those settings test different parts of the system, so their results should remain identifiable when discussing deployment. [ 16 ] Figure 5. SLoSa uses explicit constraints in data construction and model adaptation. Reproduced from Xu, 2026 . Open full-size figure . Checks can also guide generation directly. VOLTS gives a compact model tokens representing complete grounded actions and validates candidates during branching search. It returns valid plans for about 76% of 2,000 problems across four classical planning domains. The validator judges actions against the formal state and domain; it cannot supply a language requirement that was never encoded. [ 17 ] SELP translates user constraints into temporal logic and restricts planning with the selected specification. Planner-in-the-loop formalization instead diagnoses and repairs specifications written in the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL). It separates parseability, solvability and agreement with reference planning outcomes, exposing errors that a syntax check would miss. [ 18 , 19 ] These mechanisms address different errors. Training can improve the first proposal, constrained decoding can reject an inapplicable action, and planner feedback can reveal a defective specification. Their costs also differ. A smaller model making several repair calls may have worse response latency than a larger model making one successful call. When the policy learns the movement Vision-language-action models assign more of perception and control to a learned policy. RT-2 represents robot actions as tokens and combines robot demonstrations with visual-language training. Diffusion Policy generates continuous action sequences through denoising and updates them over a receding horizon. Each approach needs an action representation and experience appropriate to the robot. [ 20 , 21 ] SmolVLA combines a compact visual-language backbone with an action expert and community-collected robot data. It predicts chunks of upcoming actions and separates that prediction from execution. This is a different resource problem from interpreting a sentence into a short task record, because images and actions must also be processed at the required control rate. [ 22 ] Figure 6. SmolVLA learns the observation-to-action interface and separates prediction from execution. Reproduced from Shukor, 2025 . Open full-size figure . Adaptation choices can be as consequential as the model name. OpenVLA-OFT combines parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous actions and a regression objective. In its LIBERO evaluation, average success rises from 76.5% to 97.1% and action-generation throughput increases by 26 times. That comparison changes the training and execution recipe, so the improvement cannot be attributed to backbone size alone. [ 23 ] A learned policy and an explicit planner can also share a system. A task interpreter might select a learned grasping skill while a separate motion or collision check evaluates its proposed movement. Choosing that division requires compatible observations, action conventions and timing, rather than a parameter-count comparison between models doing different jobs. Testing outside the familiar scene The training signal determines what a system can learn. An instruction paired with a formal task trains interpretation. Camera observations paired with timed actions train behavior. MimicGen adapts object-relative demonstration segments to new configurations, generating more than 50,000 demonstrations from roughly 200 human demonstrations in its study. That expands behavioral supervision without automatically labeling every route or exclusion a person might request. [ 24 ] Simulation frameworks such as Isaac Lab provide controlled observations, actuator models and parallel rollouts. For an initial interpretation test, exact simulator object state can remove perception errors. Replacing it later with camera-derived state introduces another source of uncertainty that should be evaluated separately. [ 25 ] LIBERO separates variations in spatial arrangements, objects, goals and longer task sequences. LIBERO-Plus adds controlled perturbations of language, layout, camera view, robot initialization, lighting, backgrounds and sensor noise. These tests make a nominal success score much easier to interpret. A policy may handle the original task while relying on a familiar viewpoint or phrasing. [ 26 , 27 ] Figure 7. LIBERO-Plus tests controlled departures from nominal evaluation conditions. Reproduced from Fei, 2026 . Open full-size figure . LIBERO-Safety distinguishes physical execution risks from semantic safety assessment. Completion, collision and refusal rates need to be read together. A system that executes fewer requests may collide less without improving the movements it does attempt. RoboDojo extends evaluation across simulation and real robots, where common interfaces help expose differences in generalization, memory, precision and long-horizon execution. [ 28 , 29 ] A focused study in Visual Components A useful first study can stay with one arm and a small pick-and-place vocabulary. The interpreter identifies an object, a reference, a relation and an optional route. Deterministic code computes coordinates and calls a limited skill library. Separate observations check the carried-object trace and final placement after release. Three conditions would share the same interpreter and motion backend. A single-proposal baseline gets one attempt. A bounded-repair condition can use format and feasibility diagnostics. A requirement-checking condition also compares the proposal with requirements extracted from the original sentence before the checker sees the proposal. Separate prompting can still produce correlated mistakes, so an extra-compute control should receive the same call, token and time budget without that checker. The test cases can stay small enough to diagnose. Swap left and right, exchange object names, add a marker passage, or request an explicit gap. Then move the reference object and repeat the last successful task. A paraphrase should preserve the intended action; changing a requirement should change it. Reordering scene records or consistently renaming identifiers should also preserve the result after identities are mapped back. Task requirements must be defined independently of the model output, with valid alternative placements and routes accepted. Ambiguous or unsupported requests should trigger clarification. A failed step ends a dependent episode, leaving its remaining steps unsuccessful. Otherwise the score can improve merely by excluding the difficult parts of a workflow. Model adaptation deserves its own comparison. Start with the original model and the same model adapted on reviewed examples, holding the checker and motion backend fixed. Split task families before generating related scene variants or paraphrases. Error–correction examples can be tested under a matched training budget, with artificial mistakes kept distinct from failures actually made by the model. The main outcome is whole-request success , accompanied by requirement completeness and the fraction of reported completions that omit something requested. Record object, relation, route and context errors separately. Pair completion and refusal counts with collisions, placement error and route accuracy. Median and 95th-percentile response times should include failed requests; model inference, repairs and simulated motion should remain distinguishable. Peak memory and hardware settings complete the deployment picture. Natural language should let an operator change the task without rewriting the controller. A new waypoint must change the route, a moved reference must change the placement, and a correction must preserve every requirement that still applies. Grounding, planning and learned control provide the components; the next step is to connect them through explicit, testable interfaces that carry intent all the way into executed motion. My T2T repository puts these questions into a runnable MuJoCo KUKA iiwa cell, with Visual Components as the intended industrial target. It compares planning and requirement-checking methods on routes, placements and follow-up instructions, scoring the executed outcome. The code, frozen tasks and evaluation commands are available there for trying the approach and inspecting where it fails. References Stefanie Tellex et al. (2011). title: ChargeWise Fits the Fleet to the Grid
summary: Building ChargeWise AI with physical charging constraints, independent schedule checks, the original hosted application, Nemotron tools, and a forecasting follow-up.
text: 25 October 2026 · Energy & optimization · 8 min read ChargeWise Fits the Fleet to the Grid Updated 11 November 2026 Open the interactive demo ↗ Download the editable planner Source code ↗ Two 11 kW chargers do not necessarily require a 22 kW grid connection. The answer depends on which vehicles are plugged in, how much energy they need, and when they leave. For the Nebius × NVIDIA hackathon , I built ChargeWise AI with Muhammad Talha Toqeer and Umar Khan . A fleet manager enters the vehicles, departure times, energy requirements, and available hardware. The planner compares schedules and works out how much shared site power the configured fleet needs. [ 1 ] The live demo runs the same application as the downloadable build: the editable React dashboard, OR-Tools planner, capacity checks and guided outage workflow. Start with Load sample and Start guided demo . It uses synthetic data and controls no physical chargers. The plug stays occupied after charging ends A van can finish charging at 09:00 and remain parked until noon. Unless someone moves it, that charger cannot serve another vehicle during those three hours. A scheduler that ignores occupancy can produce an attractive power curve that the depot cannot follow. ChargeWise checks connector compatibility, physical connection and availability, charger ratings, vehicle power limits, charging efficiency, and the site's combined load. It also uses a conservative state-of-charge-dependent taper envelope. That envelope makes planning tractable; a particular vehicle's measured charging curve would describe its battery more closely. The three greedy baselines use the same physical constraints as the optimized schedule. First-come-first-served follows arrival order; earliest-deadline-first prioritises departures; least-laxity-first prioritises the vehicles with least remaining scheduling slack. Why 8.89 kW is enough for this fleet The four-van example has two fixed 11 kW ports and requires 84 battery kWh over the day. All three baselines meet every energy target and reach a 22 kW peak. The optimized schedule also meets every target, at 8.89 kW . The published fixture records an optimal solver result and independent validation. [ 2 ] The afternoon pair needs 48 battery kWh in six hours. At 90% charging efficiency, that requires 53.33 grid kWh. Even a perfectly flat schedule therefore needs at least $$P_{\min}\geq\frac{48\ \mathrm{kWh}}{6\ \mathrm{h}\times0.90}=8.888\ldots\ \mathrm{kW}.$$ A lower limit cannot supply enough energy in that window. The optimizer finds a schedule attaining the bound while meeting the configured constraints. The peak is about 60% lower than the greedy schedules. Both the infeasibility argument below the bound and a feasible schedule at the bound are available in this example. Cheap electricity can set an expensive peak If every van follows the same low-price interval, the combined load can create a new demand peak. An energy-only objective misses that part of the bill. In the four-van schedule, energy cost rises from €21.47 to €24.09 while the peak falls from 22 to 8.89 kW. At €15.20/kW/month, those peaks imply monthly demand charges of €334.40 and €135.11 if they are the billing-period maxima. The build's €355.87 and €159.20 totals add one day of energy to those full monthly charges. They are mixed-period scenario scores, not comparable daily bills or a demonstrated 55% saving. A billing comparison needs the full month, its prior peak and all site loads. For illustration, repeating these exact daily schedules for 30 days, with no other site load or earlier peak, would give about €978 for the baseline and €858 for the optimized schedule, roughly 12% lower. This calculation aligns the time bases but assumes identical days; it is not a replay of a real billing month. A previous peak changes the decision too. Once the billing period has already reached a particular demand level, pushing today's load below that level cannot reduce the established demand charge. The planner needs that history as well as the upcoming prices. Nemotron requests a replan; the solver builds it NVIDIA Nemotron, accessed through Nebius Token Factory, connects an operator's questions to application tools. It can retrieve schedule facts or request an authorised simulated charger outage. The tool changes equipment availability, OR-Tools computes a new schedule, and a separate validator checks the allocations before the assistant explains the result. In the verified CH-01 morning-outage example, the optimized peak rises from 8.89 to 10 kW and every vehicle still receives its requested energy. The architecture film below demonstrates a separate afternoon outage: CH-02 is unavailable from 16:00 to 18:00, with delivery before noon frozen. In that recorded schedule, redistributing the remaining allocations retains the 8.89 kW peak. Freezing delivered energy is essential. A replan after noon must preserve what happened in the morning. Otherwise an optimizer could appear to recover by changing a past allocation that the depot can no longer execute. Interactive architecture film. Play or scrub through input validation, scheduling, independent checks, the Nemotron tool loop, and replanning. The film uses recorded synthetic results; it does not call an LLM or run the optimizer. Open film ↗ Forecasting for the charging decision In a follow-up run on 26 October , pretrained time-series models forecast 37 locally held-out days of historical German electricity prices from August–September 2019. Chronos-Bolt Small reduced price mean absolute error by 29.2% against ridge regression. TimesFM also improved forecast accuracy. [ 3 ] Four-van replay means. Energy uses realised held-out prices; the optimizer plans against each forecast. The last column adds a full monthly demand charge to one scenario day and must not be interpreted as a daily bill. Forecast Price MAE €/MWh Energy only €/scenario-day Energy + monthly demand mixed-period score, € Ridge 7.042 3.3353 138.9116 TimesFM 2.5 200M 5.720 3.3377 138.9092 Chronos-Bolt Small 48M 4.988 3.3395 138.9095 Perfect-price oracle n/a 3.3141 138.9059 TimesFM's mean mixed-period objective is only about €0.0025 below ridge over the 37 evaluated days. No paired uncertainty interval or repeat-run analysis was reported, so this difference is too small to support a robust economic advantage. All 518 scenario/model/tariff solves passed the stated checks and met energy targets; ridge had the lowest energy-only mean among the forecasts. The models can improve prices during hours when no van is connected, or distinguish between cheap hours that the timetable makes interchangeable. A demand peak can also dominate the small differences in energy cost. Lower forecasting error therefore need not yield a useful change in the charging decision. This was an exploratory replay of old data, with unknown overlap between the evaluation period and model pretraining. Retail prices and the depot's other electrical loads were absent. Forecasts were evaluated by passing them through the physical optimizer and costing the resulting schedule against realised prices. Already published day-ahead prices should be used directly; prediction is useful only where information is still missing. Try the planner Open ChargeWise , load the sample and start the guided demo. The original dashboard lets you edit vehicles, chargers, prices and tariffs, compare schedules, check capacity and replan around simulated outages. Already delivered energy stays frozen when replanning. The hosted and downloadable versions use the same Python optimizer and independent schedule checks, including the battery taper envelope. The public demo uses the application's labelled local-summary assistant; it makes no paid model calls. The forecasting study above reports the separate historical-price evaluation. Run the full application locally The portable build contains the same dashboard and optimizer, with uploads, taper constraints and optional assistant integration. [ 4 ] With Python 3.11+ and uv installed, extract it and run: Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Node.js is unnecessary because the frontend is prebuilt. Without a configured inference provider, the assistant shows a labelled local summary of computed results. Code, data, and demo ChargeWise AI source repository . title: When Do AI Outputs Tip?
summary: One attention head tested across sixteen held-out Qwen2.5-0.5B prompts, a mathematical response clock, and cache edits that hold current answers fixed.
text:
18 October 2026 · AI research · 17 min read When Do AI Outputs Tip? Updated 11 November 2026 Reversing “red or blue” to “blue or red” moved a model's probability of answering red by 65.3 percentage points on average. Its mean probability of an incorrect answer moved by only 1.1 points. Across sixteen matched pairs, the shift toward blue helped when blue was correct and hurt when red was correct. The two effects largely cancelled in the average error. The probe was also too unreliable to study the loss of previously reliable behaviour, so I moved to a separately qualified retrieval task. Option-order sensitivity and forgetting need different measurements. The broader project asks what a model carries into its next answer. Can a small description of its computation predict several future answers and the effect of a correction? Neil F. Johnson and Frank Y. Huo's Competition for attention predicts good-to-bad tipping in AI gave me a starting model: competing representations can change which output dominates as a conversation develops. [ 1 ] What counts as tipping? A model that was wrong from the start has not lost a reliable ability. Before looking for a transition, the retrieval task has to establish that the model can answer the source question under the specified wording and decoder. The earlier option-order probe failed that purpose. The later qualification fixes a narrower setting in which an incorrect conversational history can be compared with a correct one. There are also different events hidden inside the word tipping . The most likely answer can switch when two scores cross, even while both probabilities change smoothly. A sampled conversation can make a sudden first error without any abrupt change in its underlying probabilities. Persistent wrong answers, recovery after an error, and a change in factual topic are further outcomes. A first-error clock addresses only the first failure along the declared continuation. These experiments change inference-time state with the model weights held fixed. They concern what generated history and cached computation do to later answers. They do not measure catastrophic forgetting from training on a new task, although the question of preserving some readouts while changing others connects the two problems. Which level of analysis answers the question? Level What is measured What it can establish Output behaviour Token probabilities and accepted complete answers Whether a specified answer becomes more or less likely Causal mechanism Matched edits to messages, routing or stored values Whether that intervention changes the measured behaviour Predictive state A state description updated through a continuation Whether it retains the information needed for later risks Correction choice Outcomes under available repairs, including their costs Whether extra information changes a useful decision A semantic label is often the right level for evaluating an answer, but it can hide the token-level differences that determine the next one. Conversely, a detailed attention map can show where information was read without establishing that the final answer changed. Following the computation from an internal edit through the vocabulary distribution to accepted answer sequences connects those levels. The full cache contains much more information than a single risk score, but retaining everything gives little explanation of what matters. The aim is a smaller state whose update and predictions remain valid for a stated family of questions and interventions. Its adequacy depends on the target: predicting the next error, predicting its timing, and choosing a correction can require different information. Swapping one head's message Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct read a source fact and answered a factual question. I kept an incorrect earlier answer in the visible conversation, then replaced one attention head's internal message with the message from a matched conversation containing the correct earlier answer. On sixteen held-out prompts , mean error probability fell from 3.65% to 1.33% . The selected head was layer 16, head 7, using zero-based indexing; selection used separate discovery prompts. These probabilities came from a decoder restricted to two answer tokens. They are conditional model probabilities, not error frequencies from sampled conversations. [ 2 ] The message has two components worth separating: the values carrying information and the attention weights deciding how to combine them. Replacing only the value content, while keeping the recipient's attention weights, reduced mean error to 1.26% . Replacing only the attention weights gave 3.70% . Content transfer reproduced the average rescue in this experiment; routing transfer did not. The matched donor makes this a causal test of a specific internal replacement. Separating content from routing narrows the explanation further: a change in the weighted message can come from different information being available, different weights on that information, or both. The comparison tests those replacements while keeping the other component fixed. Measured probabilities. Compare all three interventions, then filter by source colour and wording. Each line is one prompt. Open figure ↗ · Download data The location of the edit also matters. In this cached decoder, temporarily patching the final layer's attention output can change the current logits without changing stored keys or values. If the same next token is forced in both runs, their later computations receive the same cache. An edit to stored values can persist because later queries can read those values again. The rescue does not establish that this head is the sole natural cause of the error. A donor replacement may introduce a message the recipient would not normally produce, and other heads or downstream operations can compensate for it. The held-out prompts reduce the risk of reporting only the prompts used to choose the head; they do not establish transfer to another model, an unrestricted conversation, or a different intervention. The prompt-level plot also matters because an average can conceal opposite effects across source colours and wording. An attention mass for the response clock My work on continual learning and physical modelling keeps running into a related problem: a variable can describe the present accurately while omitting information needed to update it. The fixed-prototype binary attention model gives a small example. Let \(F\) be the current score margin for the incorrect answer, so its probability is \(\sigma(F/	au)\), where \(	au\) is the decoder temperature. The margin fixes the next-answer probability. The effective attention mass \(
u\) controls how strongly another correct output changes that margin. After \(j\) additional correct outputs, $$F_j =  rac{
u F + j eta}{
u + j}.$$ Here \(
u\) measures existing attention mass in units of one additional correct output. The limiting margin \( eta\) describes the future readout induced by the correct-output prototype. The construction deliberately permits \( eta>0\): a token can be correct when emitted yet add a key/value contribution that favours the wrong answer later. That destabilising feedback is an assumption of this example, not a general property of correct answers. With \(
u=4\), one more correct output receives one fifth of the updated mass; with \(
u=40\), one forty-first. Two histories can therefore start with the same error probability and evolve differently. At future answer \(j+1\), the hazard is conditional on the preceding answers being correct. Multiplying the survival probabilities gives the chance of a first error within \(H\) answers: $$\Pr(T\leq H)=1-\prod_{j=0}^{H-1}\left[1-\sigma\left(F_j/	auight)ight].$$ This is an exact construction for the stated simplified head, with fixed prototypes and no positions, residual path, MLP, or layer normalisation. It is not a fitted law for Qwen. The neural experiments still have to establish which parts survive the additional computation. Mathematical construction. Change the two attention masses while holding the current margin fixed. Both histories begin at the same risk; their conditional hazards and cumulative error probabilities can diverge. Open figure ↗ The extra mass variable explains why a current risk score can be insufficient even when it is measured exactly. Repeating every item in a history can preserve its weighted average while increasing the mass already present. One new output then moves that average less. In the construction, the current margin describes where the system is; the mass describes its resistance to the next update. For a negative initial margin and a positive limiting margin, a greedy answer switches when accumulated updates carry the margin through zero. Increasing the initial mass delays that crossing. At nonzero decoder temperature there is no single guaranteed failure time: an error can occur before the crossing or a correct answer after it. The cumulative curve integrates those conditional risks. Its survival product does not assume independent errors. The restriction to the first error makes the state update unusually simple. Before that event, every generated answer belongs to the correct prototype. Once an incorrect answer occurs, future queries and stored contributions can change. Predicting recovery or total errors then requires additional response information. Two histories can agree on every first-error probability and still differ after that first error. The clock also suggests a test that can fail. With a fixed temperature, the first three conditional hazards can identify a nonconstant candidate clock; the remaining horizons then test its predictions. Fitting each horizon separately would not test the update law. Near-constant hazards make parameter estimates unstable, and agreement would still leave open whether several neural mechanisms can produce the same curve. The time of a correction Timing matters in the measured model too. In one recorded history, re-encoding an earlier correct “Red” as “red” before a two-answer continuation improved net success by 3.31–3.70 percentage points . Applying the corresponding normalisation only after a later accepted “Red” answer had a small negative effect on whole-continuation success. That comparison was calculated post hoc from measured conditional probabilities. It shows why a correction needs a position in the sequence as well as a description of what it changes. “red”, “Red”, and a longer sentence can express the same answer but leave different token histories. Semantic correctness sums the probabilities of accepted complete sequences. A ranking of one representative vector need not rank that sum. For the later experiments I defined twelve accepted answer forms , included their end-of-answer tokens, and retained the original vocabulary normalisation. Unmeasured branches kept explicit probability bounds. Those ranges describe the contribution missing branches could make; they are not sampling confidence intervals. A two-token decoder deliberately removes much of that complexity. Renormalising over red and blue measures preference conditional on producing one of those tokens . It does not count the possibility of another word, a longer answer or an unfinished response. That makes it useful for a controlled intervention comparison, but its error percentages cannot be read as unrestricted chat failure rates. Likewise, a correction that preserves meaning can change later behaviour through its exact spelling and tokenisation. Measuring only semantic correctness at the time of the edit would miss that difference. Measuring a single next-token probability could miss a change elsewhere in the completed answer. The answer contract and evaluation horizon therefore belong in the experiment specification. Accurate prediction, a difficult baseline A 64-number description of a structured value-cache edit, combined with reference computation retained from the decoder, reconstructed 296 conditional vocabulary distributions with a largest total-variation discrepancy of about \(1.4	imes10^{-9}\). This is a numerical consistency check of a linear edit representation followed by the original nonlinear downstream computation. It is not held-out forecasting performance or evidence of a compact autonomous predictor. The CPU decoder read trained BF16 weights and computed in float64. A state-dependent correction policy improved two-answer success by roughly 0.052–0.070 percentage points over retaining the edited cache. A simpler rule, given the current complete-answer probability, chose the same correction in every tested state. Accurate prediction had not yet demonstrated a decision advantage from remembering the intervention. Prediction accuracy and decision value are separate tests. If two states have different future risks but the same best available action, distinguishing them does not improve that choice. Conversely, a small risk difference can matter when a repair has a cost close to its expected benefit. The action set, fee, horizon and failure loss determine which state differences are useful. This motivation is related to value equivalence in model-based reinforcement learning , where a model is judged by the planning quantities it preserves. [ 5 ] Holding the current answers fixed The next test changes cached state while preserving declared current readouts. A content vector is distributed across 32 cached positions . Three current queries across seven reader heads impose 21 scalar constraints on that position profile. The remaining freedom can suppress current head-message changes while retaining a response at later public queries. This uses the same geometry that makes protected subspaces useful in continual learning: a change can be invisible to one set of readouts and visible to another. The edited cache values were rounded to float32 before checking the actual output probabilities. Four contexts combined red or blue source facts with positive or explicitly negated wording. Two opposite edits per context produced eight internal states. All eight passed the frozen matching checks: Current readout Largest measured change Initial next-token distribution \(4.8	imes10^{-10}\) total variation Total probability of twelve accepted complete answers \(5.7	imes10^{-9}\) absolute probability Checks of the accepted spellings separately also found very little redistribution. Internally different states now agree on the measured current behaviour to high precision. The future semantic-error comparison is unfinished. A later head's nonzero response alone does not establish a later change in semantic correctness. The observation used by a controller therefore needs to be specified. A head message, a vocabulary distribution, and the meaning of a complete answer preserve different information. Nick Cammarata's Goodfire essay, Neural Networks Are Already Clean , argues for examining native mechanisms with their inputs and downstream readers. Its broader claims are a working hypothesis; following the actual downstream computation is useful for these experiments. [ 4 ] The next comparison gives one controller the edit description and others the matched initial readouts. It also includes a controller allowed to measure risk later and react then. If that reactive controller catches up, retaining internal state would need to justify its value through observation cost, latency, or an intervention window that closes before the next measurement. I have not established that advantage yet. The position-profile construction provides a way to ask that question without merely comparing two visibly different prompts. Current readers impose linear constraints on how a value edit is distributed across cached positions. A direction left unobserved by those readers may become visible to a different query later. Passing the linear constraints is only the construction step; checking the actual vocabulary and complete-answer probabilities after rounding is what tests whether the intended matching survived the rest of the network. Current matching has a precise scope. Agreement on three queries does not imply agreement on every question a controller could ask, and a later internal response does not by itself establish a semantic failure. A useful follow-up has to fix the observation interface before evaluation, test later complete answers, and compare correction outcomes on fresh histories. Otherwise the observer can keep acquiring measurements until the claimed hidden difference is no longer hidden. What would make the extra state useful? The strongest result would be a pair of states that a declared observer cannot distinguish, yet for which the available repairs have different best choices. That would show a limitation of the observer for this decision, rather than merely another difference inside the network. If one repair is best in both states, the observer may remain adequate despite predicting their risks imperfectly. A state-aware controller should therefore be compared with keeping the cache, always applying the repair, a rule using the current complete-answer risk, and a controller allowed to measure again later. They need the same repair options and the same accounting for measurement and intervention costs. Any gain also has to survive new prompts, new histories and changes in the allowed edits. The practical motivation is to correct a conversation before an error becomes expensive. These experiments establish a local causal rescue and a mathematical example of missing temporal information. The matched-readout experiment is an attempt to find the corresponding decision problem in a trained model. Whether its extra state provides useful advance warning remains the question being tested. References and experiment materials Johnson, N. F. & Huo, F. Y. Competition for attention predicts good-to-bad tipping in AI , 2026, preprint. Starting framework; the experiments and clock extension described here are separate work. Störk, J. Head-content versus routing intervention figure and published plotting data . Sixteen held-out prompts, three interventions, conditional two-token decoder. Störk, J. Attention-memory response clock . Interactive mathematical construction accompanying the fixed-prototype update law; no fitted neural-model results. Cammarata, N. Neural Networks Are Already Clean , Goodfire. Informal research essay and working hypothesis. Grimm, C., Barreto, A., Singh, S. & Silver, D. The Value Equivalence Principle for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning , NeurIPS 2020. title: Gold Medals Don't Stack Batteries: Building Training Grounds for AI Agents
summary: From programming medals to battery stacking: verifiable environments, six 2026 agent and robotics projects, and practical tests for learning rewards, recovery, and resets.
text: 11 October 2026 · Agents & learning Gold Medals Don't Stack Batteries: Building Training Grounds for AI Agents Updated 11 November 2026 The promise behind AI, and especially recursive self-improvement, is a system that learns from its own attempts: a programmer that becomes a better programmer, a researcher that builds better experiments, eventually a generalist that can carry a job through to completion. Where does the measuring stick hang now? In competitive programming, remarkably high. At the 2025 ICPC World Finals, OpenAI's system solved all 12 problems ; Google DeepMind's Gemini Deep Think solved 10 of 12 , reaching gold-medal level. OpenAI used a separate Local Judge experiment with the same problems and test data. University teams had three students sharing one computer, no internet access, limited reference notes, and five hours. [ 1 , 2 ] NVIDIA then reported 535.4 out of 600 on the IOI 2026 problems for a competition-specific Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC system with iterative feedback, above the top human score of 498.27. [ 3 ] Model-assisted mathematics now includes research manuscripts and proof artifacts, collected in OpenAI's public repository. Its reported runs used an average of three hours of thinking compute per result. The tasks have different histories, and the runtime excludes the human work behind the questions, model development and subsequent proof checking. [ 4 ] Coding and mathematics are useful, but you can't have a nontrivial automorphism for dinner, and a programming medal doesn't align an electrode stack (yet). A factory gives feedback very differently Consider battery stacking. A useful system has to combine camera observations, distance measurements, vacuum readings, motion commands, and alignment checks. It needs to recognise an electrode edge, pick the sheet without damaging it, place it within tolerance, and notice when the pickup did not work. These are long-horizon, messy workflows, and one mistake can invalidate the entire workflow. Agent performance on long tasks is also the subject of METR's task-horizon study. [ 5 ] This is also a hierarchy of timescales. Camera acquisition and machine control can run far faster than a language model should be asked to deliberate. The agent's job could be to select a procedure, diagnose an abnormal run, or propose a correction; fast controllers still execute bounded motions and enforce machine interlocks. Also, LLMs are far from data-efficient learners. Nastase and colleagues note that modern models train on orders of magnitude more language input than humans receive. [ 17 ] In lieu of better learning algorithms, one solution is more training, which requires an environment for that purpose. Reinforcement-learning environments An environment specifies what the agent can observe, which actions are possible, how those actions change the situation, and how success is scored. Sutton and Barto's agent–environment loop and Szepesvári's Markov decision processes already describe the core interaction. The modern packaging adds containers, tool APIs, files, and execution traces. [ 6 , 7 ] One distinction matters: the agent's observation is not necessarily the full state. A photograph may hide a misaligned lower electrode; a successful tool response may not establish that a downstream file is valid. A Markov model assumes the state contains what is needed to predict the next transition. Real agents often have to infer that state from incomplete observations and history. Textbook formulation Sutton & Barto Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction Szepesvári Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Current environment tooling The same interaction, from textbooks to practical guides: Sutton & Barto; Szepesvári; Patronus AI ; Abhilasha Gulhane's Gymnasium explainer. Open an image to read the original. Gymnasium's official implementation guide documents the interface. [ 6 – 8 ] For a tool-using agent, it is helpful to define the environment contract before choosing a training algorithm. Initial state The exact files, material batch, calibration, and machine configuration at the start. Observations and tools The readings the agent can access and the bounded actions it can request. Permissions are part of the experiment. Task and budget A concrete outcome, tolerances, and limits on time, actions, or compute. Reset A way to restore the same starting conditions without carrying accidental advantages into the next attempt. Evidence and scoring Independent checks of the resulting state, alongside a trace explaining how it was reached. Gymnasium , the Farama Foundation's Python library for reinforcement-learning environments and successor to OpenAI Gym, makes part of this contract explicit through observation and action spaces, reset() , and step(action) . Reset returns the first observation; step returns an observation, reward, termination and truncation flags, and auxiliary information. Reaching the goal and exhausting a time budget are different endings. [ 8 ] What changes when the agent learns? The environment supplies experience. The learning procedure decides what persists from it. That persistent change can live in two places. Inside the model: training changes its weights. R2E-Gym builds executable software tasks with hybrid verification to train coding agents. On-policy distillation instead trains a student on its own generated sequences using feedback from a teacher, addressing the mismatch between practising on teacher answers and generating its own at deployment. These are different ways of using experience, not interchangeable names for running a test suite. [ 9 , 10 ] Around the model: the harness changes what is stored, retrieved, called, and checked. Reflexion keeps verbal feedback in memory for later attempts; Voyager builds a library of executable skills; DSPy optimises language-model pipelines against a metric. A saved procedure can improve an agent without changing the underlying model weights. [ 11 – 13 ] Meta-Harness goes further by searching over the harness code itself, using previous candidates, scores, and execution traces. Lee and colleagues report a 7.7-point improvement on their online text-classification comparison with four times fewer context tokens, plus results on maths retrieval and agentic coding. It is a reason to measure the complete system: the same model can behave differently when its surrounding software changes. [ 14 ] COS-PLAY, from Xiyang Wu and colleagues, couples a decision agent with an evolving skill bank. Skills are extracted and refined from rollouts, while the decision agent learns to retrieve and use them. Its experiments span six game environments. That gives a concrete example of joint improvement, with demonstrated scope in games rather than battery manufacturing. [ 15 ] A benchmark can supply tasks, tools, and executable checks; using it for training additionally requires a loop that turns attempts and feedback into updates. Evaluation needs separate, held-out tasks. Repeatedly adapting to the same cases can produce a very competent specialist in that particular test suite. VERA turns recorded work into a place to practise The October 2026 VERA preprint constructs restartable environments from benchmark trajectories, workspace state, and tool specifications. Generated binary rubrics attach scores to observable evidence. A judge inspects execution and artifacts; container replay checks that the task actually runs. Executable failures override favourable judge scores. Only admitted environments enter the training bank. [ 16 ] VERA's environment admission pipeline. Figure excerpt from Liu et al. [16] . Its co-evolution loop attributes failures to model stages or harness skills. Model updates use verified rubric rewards; harness edits face paired development runs with the model frozen. Updates alternate, and rejected candidates do not replace the accepted system. Stage-wise evaluation helps locate failures; end-to-end evaluation checks the complete workflow. The reported gains concern automation and medical-research benchmarks. [ 16 ] Alternating model and harness updates. Figure excerpt from Liu et al. [16] . An agent may propose its next skill or training stage, while independent execution decides whether the change helps. Keeping a record of rejected and accepted changes makes the improvement process inspectable. Learning rewards from near-misses RoboReward (January 2026) tackles a specific data problem. Robot demonstration datasets contain many successful runs and too few failures to train a reliable judge. Lee and colleagues generate negative examples by changing the task description of a successful video and cutting videos short to represent partial progress. Their released 4B- and 8B-parameter reward models learn from successes, failures, and near-misses. The 8B model also improves policy learning in real-robot RL compared with Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 rewards, although human-provided rewards remain better in that experiment. [ 18 ] For electrode placement, near-misses are particularly useful. A sheet can reach the correct destination but be rotated, shifted, folded, or picked up together with another sheet. A training set could pair camera clips with independently measured alignment and pickup outcomes. Visual feedback would help classify the failure; the acceptance criterion would still come from the measurements. A final photograph alone cannot establish the alignment of layers hidden beneath the top sheet. Hack-Verifiable Environments (May 2026) makes the scoring problem testable. Roth and colleagues deliberately insert exploitable reward shortcuts into TextArena environments, with deterministic checks that identify whether an agent uses them. Their open-source testbed measures reward hacking directly instead of relying on retrospective judgement of a suspicious trajectory. [ 19 ] A manufacturing adaptation could include an editable success report alongside protected sensor records, or an apparently favourable but outdated camera frame. The test would record whether the agent accepts the shortcut, requests fresh evidence, or stops. Recovery needs its own training data FLARE (CVPR 2026) separates errors that permit a retry from failures that require the scene to be reset. Its training demonstrations include perturbed robot poses and bridging motions, so a vision-language-action policy learns to resume after execution deviates from the successful trajectory. For larger failures, offline video analysis identifies broken task states and guides the collection of object-specific reset skills. An online multimodal monitor then chooses between continuing the task and invoking a reset skill. [ 20 ] In a stacking cell, a missed pickup may permit another attempt; a dropped or damaged sheet may require removal and a verified restart. Those are different recovery tasks and need different examples. REVOLVE (September 2026) puts correction, reset, and retraining into one real-robot loop. Its four tasks include sorting workpieces, throwing paper, pouring water, and ringing a bell. Each starts with 100 demonstrations ; subsequent rounds add successful runs and failure-correction trajectories. Across five iterations, average task success rises from 40% to 58.5% , an increase of 18.5 percentage points. The reset policies succeed in 98% of 200 trials . In the authors' human-effort comparison, data collection falls from 8.89 to 0.50 hours and deployment testing from 2.67 to 0.13 hours. These results concern their four configured tasks, with task-specific reset policies generated and manually refined beforehand. [ 21 ] Resetting is therefore part of the training infrastructure, with its own failure rate and labour cost. For a sheet-handling experiment, each episode should record recovery success, reset time, discarded sheets, and operator interventions. An agent that improves pickup success but doubles the time needed to restore the cell may make training more expensive. Reset failures should also be recorded separately from failures of the task policy. Building and testing a manufacturing environment NVIDIA's July 2026 Isaac GR00T development workflow provides a concrete implementation route. Isaac Lab-Arena hosts the scene; teleoperation produces demonstrations; recordings are converted into LeRobot format; GR00T is post-trained and evaluated in closed-loop rollouts. The tutorial uses 400 demonstrations for its example and tunes the visual components and action model while freezing the language model. It also distinguishes a one-episode smoke test from a success-rate estimate over 100 or 1,000 complete episodes . [ 22 ] An electrode-handling version would need its own sheet mechanics, vacuum behaviour, sensors, and tooling; the available robot workflow supplies the software structure. A first environment could focus on one sheet and a small set of controlled pickup and placement faults. The table below is a proposed test design, rather than a result reported by these projects. It brings together 42 simulation tasks, 18 real-world tasks, and 30 integrated policies . The simulation suite explicitly tests generalisation, memory, precision, long-horizon execution, and open-vocabulary instructions. Its real-world evaluation system standardises hardware, resets, deployment, and the evaluation protocol. [ 23 ] For manufacturing, the corresponding test split could withhold material batches, lighting conditions, and fault combinations, then repeat selected cases on a test stand. Simulation and physical results should be reported separately. That produces a concrete comparison between the original policy, a revised harness around the same model, and a retrained model using the original harness. Accepted placements per hour, false acceptance of defective sheets, material loss, and intervention time would decide which changes are useful.
