I kept playing a field that had already moved. If you want to feel the seats yourself, the three games are playable here .

title: Finding a Fair Evaluation Under Changing Representations
summary: A proposed matched-input task for testing representation adaptation, with a frozen-feature ceiling, separate retention audits and resource-matched baselines.
text: 23 August 2026 · Continual learning Finding a Fair Evaluation Under Changing Representations Updated 11 November 2026 A strong frozen encoder can make a continual-learning benchmark easy for a new readout, even when the benchmark is intended to test representation learning. Evaluating retention under changing features therefore needs a task whose labels are present in the input but missing from the frozen representation. The construction below is a proposed experiment, with no comparative results reported yet. Keep the information in the shared input Suppose each image carries coarse stripes identifying a group and fine stripes identifying a class within that group. Both frozen and adaptive models receive the identical, unblurred image. The frozen baseline keeps its encoder fixed and learns a readout; the adaptive model starts from the same encoder and may change its filters before downsampling. Architecture, data access, head capacity and training budgets must be reported separately. If the frozen encoder maps all k classes in a balanced group to exactly the same feature vector, any classifier using only that vector is capped at 1/k accuracy within the group. For an unbalanced group the ceiling is the largest class prior. That ceiling concerns the encoder's output, not missing information in the raw image. Applying the same irreversible low-pass filter to both models' inputs would destroy the fine labels for everyone; adaptation could not recover them. The frozen encoder discards the fine stripe information. Both competitors must receive the original images; an adaptive encoder must be allowed to change its filters before this bottleneck. Blurring the shared input would make the task unsolvable for both. A concrete implementation would first verify the feature collision, including aliasing checks. It would then train the same architecture from the shared initialisation to check that changing the pre-downsampling filters actually recovers the labels. An architectural possibility is not a successful training result. If that adaptive control fails, the proposed benchmark has not yet established the intended separation. Measure acquisition and retention separately For each method, report new-task accuracy, the change in old-task loss or accuracy, retained memory, update cost and variability across seeds. A strong frozen baseline remains necessary. In a task with an adapting advantage, the next question is how much of that advantage survives an explicit retention constraint. For a declared candidate set \(\mathcal M\), define \(\mathcal R_\epsilon\) as the candidates passing a preregistered retention audit. For example, a simultaneous upper confidence bound on every old task's loss increase must be at most \(\epsilon\), with the confidence level and treatment of multiple comparisons fixed in advance. An empirical adaptation–retention gap is then $$\mathrm{EARG}_{\mathcal M,\epsilon}=\max_{m\in\mathcal M}\widehat{\mathrm{acc}}(m)-\max_{m\in\mathcal R_\epsilon}\widehat{\mathrm{acc}}(m).$$ The gap depends on the candidate set, test distribution, tolerance and audit uncertainty. It is undefined if no candidate passes. Held-out checks provide statistical evidence on that distribution; they are not a formal retention certificate. A mathematical certificate would additionally need an explicit bound, its assumptions and a proof that they hold for the evaluated updates. Model selection and the final audit also need separate data. Compare the methods that address each failure EWC and Synaptic Intelligence regularise changes to important parameters. Learning without Forgetting uses output distillation. A-GEM projects gradients using an episodic example memory; it is itself a memory-based method. GPM stores activation-derived subspaces and projects updates against them. These mechanisms constrain different quantities and deserve separate baselines. There are no measurements here supporting a claim that all five collapse when representations adapt. [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] Replay can re-evaluate old examples in the new representation, while distillation and stored-subspace methods preserve summaries of earlier behaviour. The relevant comparison is how each handles the same feature change at matched resource budgets. Reporting accuracy alone would hide the different storage, privacy and compute costs. Memory is a deployment choice Jung and colleagues' Compact Memory for Continual Logistic Regression builds a Hessian-matching summary for a fixed-feature logistic model. On Split-ImageNet, memory equivalent to 0.3% of the dataset gives about 60% accuracy versus 30% for experience replay; increasing memory to 2% gives 74%, against a 77.6% batch baseline. That is a compact stored summary, not zero memory or evidence that all end-to-end models need no exemplars. [ 1 ] Cho and colleagues' Forget Forgetting instead studies abundant-memory regimes where GPU time is the tighter constraint. Its replay baselines are competitive, and Weight Space Consolidation targets the remaining plasticity problem. Replay is therefore an important practical baseline. Exemplar-free methods matter where raw-data retention, privacy, bandwidth or storage actually restrict deployment; those restrictions must be specified rather than assumed universal. [ 2 ] How this relates to IGFA My IGFA experiments use Rotated-Digits with a frozen backbone. They test interference control within a fixed feature space, the restricted setting in which the geometric argument is easiest to check. They do not evaluate retention under an adapting encoder. The proposed stripe experiment asks a harder, complementary question and still needs its adaptive control, matched method runs and held-out retention audit.

title: The Student Becomes the Teacher
summary: Self-distillation transfers a model’s own supervision. Majority pseudo-labels can correct minority errors or reinforce systematic mistakes; flatness alone guarantees neither generalisation nor retention.
text: 16 August 2026 · AI research The Student Becomes the Teacher Updated 11 November 2026 Reading notes on self-distillation without labels (OPSD, U-OPSD, L-OPSD). In battery research, a single ground-truth requires assembling a cell, cycling it for weeks, and extracting one electrochemical data point. This consumes both time and money and post-training large language models has the exact same problem. Verified reasoning traces, gold answers, and external reward models are the labels, and they are just as scarce relative to the volume of data a model could learn from. This week, both Guibin Zhang from NUS and Yijiang Li from UC San Diego pushed the question "what if the model supplies its own supervision". Short answer: the external teacher (OPSD), the ground-truth labels (U-OPSD), and now handcrafted privileged context have all been replaced by the model itself. Background: one model, two contexts The line of work starts with On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD, January 2026, arXiv:2601.18734 ). A single LLM acts as both teacher and student under different contexts. The teacher conditions on privileged information (verified reasoning traces) while the student sees only the question. Training minimizes the per-token divergence between the two distributions over the student's own rollouts, on trajectories it would actually produce. Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) applies the same trick to demonstrations: the demonstration-conditioned model becomes its own teacher, generating on-policy training signals that, in the original experiments, preserved prior capabilities better than ordinary SFT while acquiring new skills. It was one of the papers put through the ICML 2026 open reproduction effort ( Hugging Face report ), I come back to that below. Remove or learn the supervision U-OPSD , On-Policy Self-Distillation without any Supervision arXiv:2608.06296 removes the last external crutch. Sample k rollouts, majority-vote a pseudo-solution, gate it by a self-consistency threshold, then condition the model on that pseudo-solution and distill only on the disagreeing completions. The model trains disagreeing rollouts toward its majority pseudo-answer. This can repair minority mistakes when the majority is correct; a confident but wrong majority instead reinforces the error. An answer the model produces consistently is treated as correct, the agreement among samples is taken as evidence (in place of any external check). On Qwen3 math in non-thinking mode, U-OPSD beats supervised OPSD by up to 3.2 points and GRPO by up to 8.9 points ( summary ), using no labels at all. Interactive · Majority vote is not truth Each rollout answers correctly with probability p. When it is wrong, correlated blind spots (ρ) push it toward the same wrong answer. Watch the vote lock in. Per-rollout accuracy p 45% Error correlation ρ 0.60 Consistency (top share) … Pseudo-label … Replay Monte Carlo over four answers (A is the truth). The pseudo-label locks when the leading answer crosses the 60% consistency threshold. Raise ρ and consensus can converge, confidently, on a wrong answer. L-OPSD , Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation arXiv:2608.13040 steps in the opposite direction. Instead of removing the privileged context, it makes privilege learnable: retrieved experiences are composed into continuous latent tokens that condition the self-teacher and dense supervision is provided at every visited prefix. Because the composer is trainable, the distillation loss has a degenerate minimum (the teacher collapses into the student for uninformative context). The privileged-margin objective forbids this by requiring the teacher to maintain a verifiable log-probability advantage over the student on successful trajectories. The latent context must stay informative, not merely easy to match. Without the constraint, joint training performs worse than freezing the composer outright. With this constraint, L-OPSD outperforms GRPO, OPSD, SDPO, and Skill-SD on agentic tool use and code generation, using under 30% of GRPO's rollout budget. Interactive · The degenerate basin A toy distillation loss with two minima: an informative-context basin (good) and a teacher-equals-student mirror (degenerate). Raise the margin to fill the mirror, or drag the hollow start marker to probe the basins live. Privileged margin m 0.030 Basin reached … Task score … Reroutes to informative at … Replay descent Schematic landscape. The margin penalty fills the mirror basin; past a critical m the descent reroutes to the informative one. Endpoint scores 0.551 (mirror) and 0.637 (informative) are the paper's ablation. One paper removes privileged information entirely, the other learns to construct it. Which algorithm wins depends on the failure mode you're more afraid of; the model confidently agreeing with its own mistakes vs. the teacher collapsing into a mirror of the student. Some limitations The privilege illusion. The DAPD analysis ( coverage ) argues that OPSD quietly teaches the student to behave as if the reference were still present at inference time. The measured consequence: gains of +5.19 points at 1.7B parameters collapse to ≤ +0.28 at 8B–32B. What works at small scale may be an artifact of scale. Decoding collapse. In agentic settings, feedback-augmented self-distillation can produce trajectories that look diverse but are largely input-agnostic templates. The KL-based supervision signal becomes uninformative, and standard evaluation metrics miss it ( arXiv:2607.17558 ). An exponential-moving-average teacher is a partial fix. The awkward reproduction. In the ICML 2026 open reproduction challenge, at least one independent attempt found no SDFT advantage over matched SFT on a 507-example science evaluation, leaving toy-scale support only for the reduced-forgetting claim ( reproduction logbooks ). One reproduction is not a refutation, but it is exactly the kind of result that should be cited next to the original. These failures concern both the learning signal and how it is evaluated. Self-generated supervision inherits the model's blind spots. Majority voting can reduce uncorrelated mistakes, but correlated wrong answers can become more consistent under training. An independent check or environment reward addresses a different problem from agreement among samples. Why I care Process–property models in electrode manufacturing have the same structure as this problem: abundant process data from coating and calendering lines, scarce and delayed electrochemical labels from cycling tests. Any method that extracts training signal from internal consistency rather than external labels is directly relevant to surrogate models that have to stay useful between cycling campaigns. The SDFT thread also connects to my continual-learning work. On-policy self-signals reduce forgetting relative to off-policy SFT, which makes them a candidate complement to structural protection mechanisms like the interference-gated approach I wrote about earlier . A speculative extension: could majority-vote pseudo-labels over process-parameter rollouts bootstrap a surrogate model during the weeks while a cycling campaign is still running? The failure modes above, especially confident systematic error, are exactly what a battery surrogate would exhibit under process drift, so the caveats transfer along with the method. A geometric caution Small output KL divergence on sampled prefixes does not imply small parameter drift or preservation of untested tasks. Flatness, parameter distance and functional retention are different properties. An argument connecting them needs assumptions about the data distribution, parameterisation and objective. Schliserman, Vansover-Hager and Koren's Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization constructs smooth convex examples where flat empirical minima have non-vanishing population risk, Ω(1), while sharp minima generalise optimally. It also analyses sharpness-aware algorithms. The result is about generalisation, not retention during self-distillation. It rules out treating flatness alone as a universal guarantee; retention still needs direct old-task measurements. Self-distillation can transfer useful behaviour without a separate teacher model. Its reliability depends on what makes the training target trustworthy, how correlated the errors are, and whether held-out tasks improve after the update. Next post From Simulating Speech to Optimizing Reasoning

title: From Simulating Speech to Optimizing Reasoning
summary: What latent steering, multiplex tokens and compressed plans establish about reasoning, with measured hint acknowledgement and task-specific limits.
text: 9 August 2026 · AI research From Simulating Speech to Optimizing Reasoning Updated 11 November 2026 Reading notes on the 2026 latent-reasoning literature. Chain-of-thought lets a model write intermediate steps before answering. Those tokens can improve performance and provide material for checking a result. They are also an incomplete record of the computation that produced them. Recent work asks which parts of reasoning can be steered, compressed or represented without committing to a full sentence at every step. What interventions can establish He and colleagues use sparse autoencoders to identify latent features associated with reasoning behaviour. Steering a small number of features can induce CoT-like behaviour without an explicit CoT prompt, while suppressing them can impair performance. That provides causal evidence for the features in the tested models. It does not show that intermediate text is unnecessary for every task or that reasoning is independent of language. [ 1 ] Turpin and colleagues show that biasing features in a prompt can alter an answer without appearing in the explanation. Anthropic extends that approach to reasoning models and six hint types. The published averages are 25% hint acknowledgement for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1 when the hint influenced the answer. Some individual settings fall below 20%; there is no universal 20% ceiling. Outcome-based RL initially improves acknowledgement in their training experiment and then plateaus. [ 2 , 4 ] Means across hint types in Anthropic's experiment, conditional on hint influence. These measure disclosure of the tested hints, not the fraction of all reasoning that is faithful. [ 4 ] The experiment tests disclosure of a known influence. A useful monitor should therefore be checked against controlled interventions, instead of assuming that a plausible explanation includes every cause of the answer. Conversely, a missing disclosure cannot establish that all visible reasoning is causally irrelevant. Pfau, Merrill and Bowman train transformers on controlled algorithmic tasks where repeated filler tokens provide useful additional computation steps. That demonstrates a role for sequential computation beyond the semantic content of the trace in those tasks. It does not establish that filler can replace mathematical working in a general-purpose model. [ 3 ] Keeping several next steps in one vector Multiplex Thinking samples several candidate next tokens and combines their embeddings into a continuous multiplex token. A confident distribution approaches an ordinary discrete step; an uncertain distribution can retain several candidates without adding sequence positions. On-policy RL trains these trajectories. Tang and colleagues report shorter sequences and gains against their discrete-CoT and RL baselines on mathematics benchmarks. [ 5 ] This changes the representation of the intermediate computation. It is not literal quantum superposition, and a mixture of embeddings need not preserve every property of separate search branches. The interesting comparison is whether the method improves success at matched inference cost, including the candidate sampling and training it requires. Compact plans that remain verbalizable Fast-ThinkAct distils textual reasoning into compact latent plans for vision-language-action policies. The representation deliberately remains verbalizable: a decoder can translate it back into language. Huang and colleagues report up to 89.3% lower inference latency than their reasoning-VLA baselines, with results on manipulation and reasoning tasks. The mechanism is useful evidence for compressing a planning interface while retaining a language link, rather than evidence that language never contributed to reasoning. [ 6 ] For manufacturing, this suggests distilling repeated planning into a small, fast representation while evaluating the resulting actions and the decoded plan separately. A verbalizer offers an inspection interface; its faithfulness still needs its own test against what changes the action. How much intermediate computation helps? Wu and colleagues find an inverted-U relationship between trace length and accuracy in their settings: additional steps help up to an optimum and can hurt beyond it. The optimum depends on task difficulty and model capability. That is an argument for selecting an appropriate reasoning budget, not for concluding that useful reasoning was never in the generated steps. [ 7 ] Interactive · Choosing a reasoning budget A toy curve illustrates an intermediate optimum in reasoning length. Change the length and an assumed capability parameter to see the trade-off; the curves are not measurements from a particular model. Reasoning length 300 tok Model capability Base Accuracy … Optimal length … Illustrative functional form, motivated by the inverted-U patterns in Wu et al. The peak positions and percentages are chosen for the demonstration, not fitted measurements or a universal law. A useful budget comparison holds the problem distribution, decoding conditions and total cost accounting fixed. It should report correct answers per token or per second alongside accuracy, and distinguish a longer sampled trace from an intervention that actually gives the model more useful computation. A claim about an optimum requires a measured cost–accuracy curve for the task and model under comparison. Agent loops and correlated errors ReAct combines generated reasoning and actions with observations returned by an environment. The runtime executes tool calls, enforces permissions and returns results; the model uses those observations to choose subsequent actions. This feedback loop can solve tasks that a single ungrounded completion cannot. Calling it a loop does not settle how competent its policy is. [ 8 ] Constrained decoding can enforce JSON or a grammar during generation. A missing comma is therefore an avoidable interface failure, not a fundamental limitation of tool use. Schema-valid requests can still choose the wrong tool, use incorrect arguments or misinterpret an observation. Those semantic failures need validators and task-level checks. [ 9 ] Yang and colleagues study diminishing returns when agents produce highly correlated evidence. Their heterogeneity includes models, prompts and tools, not just different model weights. Additional calls from one model can help, but agent count alone does not determine the gain. The relevant experiment compares complementary information and cost against an equally resourced single-agent baseline. [ 10 ] Reward the property being monitored VERITAS adds turn-level rewards for faithfulness in agentic search, distinguishing links between reasoning, search, retrieved information and the final answer. It improves the authors' measured faithfulness and task performance against outcome-only training. Those metrics concern evidence traceability in retrieval-augmented generation; they do not certify disclosure of every internal influence or predict a particular curve against a reasoning-effort slider. [ 11 ] Latent steering, multiplex tokens and distilled plans offer different ways to use intermediate computation. Their practical value can be tested through task success, latency, training cost and response to interventions. For a process-control application, the decisive comparison is whether the faster plan still chooses a valid action and exposes enough evidence to diagnose a failure.

title: The Race to O(n)
summary: Sparse patterns, DSA indexing, recurrent memory and conditional complexity bounds, with vendor claims separated from independent architectural evidence.
text: 2 August 2026 · ML systems The Race to O(n) Updated 11 November 2026 Reading notes across the subquadratic-attention literature. Dense self-attention compares token pairs, giving quadratic arithmetic cost in sequence length at fixed head dimension. Materialising its score matrix also takes quadratic memory; IO-aware implementations can avoid that allocation. Longformer, BigBird and linear attention were already tackling this in 2020, well before hundred-thousand-token contexts became common. Longer windows made the trade-offs more expensive, rather than starting the research programme. [ 1 , 3 , 4 , 7 , 9 ] Family 1: keep the comparisons, prune them Fixed sparse patterns compute only selected entries of the attention matrix. Longformer combines local windows with global tokens; BigBird adds random connections. BigBird proves universal approximation and Turing completeness under its assumptions, but those results do not promise equal efficiency at fixed depth. Appendix C constructs a task solvable by dense attention in a constant number of layers that requires nearly linear depth for sparse attention under standard complexity assumptions. Missing direct connections can therefore be costly even when eventual expressivity is preserved. [ 3 , 4 ] FlashAttention tiles exact attention into on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax, avoiding a full score matrix in GPU memory. At fixed head dimension this brings auxiliary memory down to linear in sequence length while retaining quadratic arithmetic. Its speedup comes from reduced memory traffic. [ 7 ] The cost plot below is an illustrative operation-count model, not a hardware benchmark. Its selector crossover is a chosen configuration parameter. Interactive · Where the quadratic hides Dense attention is O(T²); a linear-memory model is O(T). A learned selector adds a full-attention indexer on top of a sparse read, so on a log–log plot it runs parallel to dense (same slope 2), not to linear. Sequence length T 1.0M Dense O(T²) … Linear O(T) … Learned selector … Operations per layer, order of magnitude. Illustrative scaling at fixed dimensions, with dense cost proportional to T² and recurrent cost to T. The selector adds pairwise scoring; its 52K crossover is an assumed coefficient, not a measured limit. Family 2: learn what to prune, and pay for the learning DeepSeek's Native Sparse Attention (NSA, February 2025) combines compressed blocks, selected blocks and a sliding window in a natively trainable design. DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), introduced with V3.2-Exp in September 2025, is a separate mechanism. DSA uses the Lightning Indexer to score candidate keys and select a fine-grained sparse read. The indexer belongs to DSA, not NSA. [ 31 , 53 ] DSA's indexer scores query-key pairs with a cheaper scoring function than the main attention operation. Scoring all earlier keys still gives quadratic prefill work at fixed indexer dimensions, even when the selected read has a fixed budget. This matters for asymptotic scaling, but it does not cancel practical speedups at deployed lengths. The 52K crossover and 16×/190× overhead ratios quoted in SubQ's report are the vendor's estimates for particular configurations, not independent measurements or properties of NSA. [ 6 , 53 ] A separate routing-absorption study asks whether a trained gate improves over a frozen random gate at matched sparsity. In its controlled 31M-parameter experiment, soft joint gating gives perplexities of 48.73 and 49.83; hard top-k gating gives 71.22 and 71.24. Those measurements identify a failure mode in that setup. They do not show that every production selector, or NSA and DSA specifically, has failed to learn useful routing. Hard top-k indices have zero derivative almost everywhere, but auxiliary losses, soft routes and staged training can still train the surrounding selector. [ 26 ] Different architectures handle routing differently. Reformer uses locality-sensitive hashing; Routing Transformer updates clustering statistics; H-Transformer-1D uses a continuous hierarchical approximation. DSA uses indexer distillation and sparse-model training, and NSA supplies its own multi-branch training design. These are alternatives to test against the routing-absorption failure mode, not evidence that successful systems universally avoid hard selection or joint training. [ 31 , 33 , 35 , 36 , 53 ] Interactive · Does the gate learn anything? The routing-absorption test compares a trained gate against a frozen, never-trained random gate at matched sparsity. If the trained one barely wins, the network routed around the gate rather than through it. Switch the gate regime: Soft gate, joint Hard top-k, joint Learned − random gap … Verdict … Perplexity, lower is better (from the routing-absorption paper). Joint hard-gating makes learned and random gates numerically indistinguishable; decoupled training improves this controlled experiment, without establishing a universal ranking of sparse-attention training methods. Family 3: replace comparison with a running memory A third family doesn't prune the O(T²) computation. The pairwise comparison structure is eliminated entirely. The kernel trick is to factor the similarity between a query and key as an inner product of feature maps, φ(q)ᵀφ(k), then reorder the double sum in attention so a query only ever touches one fixed-size matrix, never the T individual keys that produced it [ 9 ] . That matrix, W, is a running memory where each token adds an outer product of its value and feature-mapped key, and each output is one read against the current W. Training cost drops to linear in T, and inference per token becomes constant time [ 9 ] . This is also a description of a linear RNN. Some popular architectures are RetNet's retention mechanism with an explicit recurrent/parallel/chunkwise duality [ 10 , 11 ] ; RWKV's receptance-weighted recurrence, built to combine transformer-style parallel training with RNN-style constant-memory inference [ 12 , 13 ] ; Griffin's RG-LRU gated linear recurrence, no attention at all in the "Hawk" variant [ 14 ] ; S4's structured state-space parameterization, made input-selective by Mamba [ 15 , 16 , 37 ] . Mamba-2's State Space Duality result is the cleanest unification: a structured class of SSMs is exactly a form of linear attention with a semiseparable causal mask, so the same computation can be read either as a cheap recurrence or as a quadratic matrix multiply, and systems tricks transfer between the two readings [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . That unification matters because it means this family's fixed-size state absorbing an unbounded sequence is a compression, and compression is lossy [ 6 ] . Family 4: don't just accumulate, correct Naive linear attention just writes forever: W ← W + v⊗κ, with nothing to un-write, so old associations linger and interfere with new writes to overlapping key directions [ 20 ] . DeltaNet asks (before writing) what the memory already predicts for the current key, and writes only the residual (one step of online gradient descent on a reconstruction loss) [ 20 , 21 ] . The error-correction needs its own hardware-efficient parallelization: a chunked, WY-representation form of the delta rule (before it scales past toy sizes) [ 21 , 22 ] . DeltaNet still can't clear memory in bulk; every correction is local to one key. The lineage adds bulk forgetting one control dimension at a time. Gated DeltaNet applies a scalar decay to the whole memory before the delta-rule correction [ 23 ] ; Kimi Delta Attention makes that decay channel-wise, so some feature subspaces are retained while others are aggressively cleared [ 24 ] ; Gated DeltaNet-2 decouples the erase gate (which key-feature channels get removed) from the write gate (which value channels get committed), previously controlled by the same scalar [ 25 ] ; CARVE argues Gated DeltaNet-2's gating is still over-parameterized relative to what a single hardware-friendly triangular solve supports, and restricts gating to the key axis to preserve that solve while conditioning erasure on the previous chunk's own content [ 38 ] . Each step is legible as one more knob on the same fast-weight object, motivated by a specific failure the previous step couldn't fix. Family 5: prove the ceiling instead of chasing it A fifth line of work stops optimizing architecture and asks how bad the fixed-size-state constraint fundamentally is. Jelassi et al. show theoretically that a two-layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while any fixed-state generalized state-space model is bounded regardless of depth or training, and confirm empirically that pretrained transformers dramatically outperform pretrained SSMs at copying and retrieving context [ 39 ] . Zoology frames the same gap as a recall–throughput trade-off: a bounded state cannot do content-addressed recall beyond roughly its own dimension, however cleverly it's gated [ 27 , 28 ] . Mimetic initialization shows that the right initialization lets Mamba copy and recall over sequences several times longer than standard init achieves, but the gap to attention narrows rather than closes [ 29 ] . BASED responds pragmatically, combining cheap-but-imprecise linear attention with exact softmax attention in a small sliding window, tuning the window to trace the recall–memory Pareto frontier rather than picking one point [ 40 ] . Log-linear attention takes the more theoretical middle path: let the number of hidden states grow logarithmically with sequence length instead of staying fixed, admitting a matmul-rich parallel form at log-linear compute cost [ 41 ] . Alman and Yu establish a conditional lower bound for document-similarity tasks that transformers can implement. Under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), those tasks admit no truly subquadratic algorithm in the specified regime. This is a worst-case forward-computation result, not a backward-pass theorem or an unconditional impossibility proof. [ 42 ] Alman and Song separately study attention gradients: almost-linear approximation is possible in a bounded-entry regime, while a SETH-based lower bound applies beyond it. The dimensions, entry bounds and approximation tolerance are part of the theorem. [ 54 ] Efficient architectures can still be useful by changing the task, accuracy target or resource trade-off. The claim that all four properties can be had at once Subquadratic AI's May 2026 report claims that its SSA selector is content-dependent and subquadratic including selection. The vendor reports 99.12% on 13-task RULER at 128K, 100% single-needle retrieval through 2M, and 98% retrieval at 12M after training at 1M, at a 0.13% attention budget. Its claimed 17× and 191× selector savings against DSA's Lightning Indexer are comparisons from the same report. These figures need independent replication and matched evaluation before they establish an advantage over competitors. [ 6 ] The public report omits the selector mechanism and records a trade-off between retrieval-optimised checkpoints and multi-document synthesis or contract analysis. It also describes switching the primary development signal to RULER. [ 6 ] Publishing the selector, its full training cost, matched baselines and held-out task results would make the claim substantially easier to assess. A useful diagnostic would compare SSA's trained selector with frozen and random selectors at matched sparsity. The routing-absorption study motivates that comparison; it cannot establish how an undisclosed SSA mechanism behaves. [ 26 ] An orthogonal axis: sharing across depth, not just across sequence Every mechanism above is about sequence mixing within a layer. A separate failure mode is dilution across layers: information written at layer 3 can be hard to recover by layer 20, because each layer only sees what survived the residual stream above it. For softmax stacks, value-residual learning feeds an early layer's attention values forward into later layers to counteract this over-smoothing [ 46 , 47 ] ; Mixture-of-Depths lets tokens skip layers entirely via a learned router instead [ 48 , 49 ] . Applying a full depth-attention operator to a linear-memory stack partially defeats the point, though (reintroduces quadratic-ish cost across depth). Tommaso Cerruti from ETH Zürich, along with Tim Rieder, George Rowlands and Lingfeng Jin, test the DeltaNet-flavored answer. They forward a lower layer's write error into the next layer's value target (Cross-Layer Error Residuals). This doesn't beat a matched baseline, because the routed error lands in the receiver's independently-learned value space, misaligned with that layer's own geometry, competing with rather than complementing its write target [ 50 ] . They (i) route into the shared residual stream instead, through a zero-initialized projection so the routed contribution starts at exactly zero and the model learns how strongly to use it; and separately, (ii) route the write value rather than the write error . That Cross-Layer Value Routing (CLVR) lowers final validation loss for both DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet hosts. It cleanly establishes sharing across depth helps specifically where the naive version of it fails and that the fix is a change of injection space. The same paper's broader sweep found that a hybrid stack (one softmax layer per two linear-memory layers) beat every pure recurrent configuration tested [ 50 ] , echoing the MiniMax M1-to-M2 story at a much smaller scale. The throughline The recurring engineering questions concern different boundaries. Does content-aware routing beat a random selector? What does selection itself cost? Does cross-layer information arrive in a representation the next layer can use? The routing study, DSA and CLVR address different parts of that problem. Matched ablations and complete cost accounting are needed to connect their results; the SubQ comparison remains a vendor claim. [ 26 , 50 , 53 ] The shape of this problem looked familiar to me. The race to O(n) and continual learning asks a structurally identical question (across tasks instead of depth or token position) whether an update from a new process regime genuinely generalizes or gets absorbed and overwritten by what an earlier regime already encoded, depending on whether it's expressed in a shared geometry the receiver can actually use [ 51 , 52 ] .

title: Lithium Dendrites Are Batteries' Dandelions
summary: A lithium-and-sodium dendrite model linking defect geometry, fracture and electronic leakage, with an explicit sodium example and unresolved current-scale mismatch.
text: 26 July 2026 · Materials Lithium Dendrites Are Batteries' Dandelions Updated 11 November 2026 On Ansgar Lowack, An Analytical Model of Critical and Subcritical Alkali Metal Dendrite Growth in Ceramic Solid Electrolytes ( arXiv:2603.20113 ). Rigid ceramic electrolytes can still be penetrated by metal-filled cracks. Lowack's analytical preprint models lithium and sodium deposition into pre-existing interfacial defects, balancing electrical dissipation against creep and crack opening. Its numerical example uses sodium and Na 5 SmSi 4 O 12 , so the quantitative example below is a sodium-system calculation rather than a lithium prediction. [ 1 ] Pressure, creep and fracture Depositing metal inside a confined defect adds volume. Soft alkali metal can accommodate some of it by creep; when confinement prevents that relief, pressure can drive the ceramic crack forward. The model combines this fracture cost with the electrical advantage of depositing at an existing conductive tip. It assumes a thin, metal-filled defect with an idealised geometry and material properties. [ 1 ] A root widening a pavement crack offers a limited visual analogy. Both involve growth in an existing confined space and the resistance of the surrounding material. Roots also respond to moisture, oxygen and biology, and tree-root pavement observations do not establish a dendrite law or a dandelion-specific weakest-link distribution. [ 2 ] The electrical and mechanical balance Onsager's variational framework constrains a coupled dissipative system. It does not say that all current follows a single path of least resistance: current distributes across available paths. In this model, the current field, deposition and mechanical dissipation are treated together. The break-even between the electrical benefit of tip deposition and the cost of crack opening gives the critical-current estimate. [ 1 ] $$J_\mathrm{crit}\approx Y\,\frac{\sigma V_M K_{Ic}}{F c_\mathrm{max}^{3/2}}.$$ Here σ is ionic conductivity, V M the alkali-metal molar volume, K Ic fracture toughness, F the Faraday constant and Y a geometry factor. The expression applies when the longest defect c max is sufficiently thin to constrain creep. Under those assumptions, doubling its length lowers the estimated threshold by a factor 2 3/2 . A distribution of independent defect lengths can then produce a Weibull-like distribution of critical currents. [ 1 ] Interactive · The weakest defect sets the limit Critical current density scales as c max −3/2 , so a single long, thin defect dominates. Drag it and watch J crit collapse. Longest defect c max 30 µm J crit (model) … vs. measured ≈ 1 mA/cm² … Schematic J crit ∝ c max −3/2 , scaled so the FESEM defect size (~30 µm) sits near the model's ~50 mA/cm². The model runs one to two orders above the measured ~1 mA/cm² band, exactly the gap the paper flags. Growth below the critical current Residual electronic conduction can permit recombination and deposition at a defect tip below the critical-fracture threshold. The paper's stress-corrosion model gives $$J_\mathrm{subcrit}\approx\frac{Y\sigma V_M K_{Iscc}}{F c_\mathrm{max}^{3/2}},\qquad K_{Iscc}=\frac{E_f\sqrt{2\pi a}}{V_M}.$$ The formation-energy term E f and electron-jump distance a determine this lower threshold. The electron transference number t e does not appear in it. Instead, t e enters the estimated failure time, approximately τ fail = Fw²/(t e V M Jc 0 ) under the paper's additional geometric approximations. Reducing electron leakage lengthens that time and suppresses this pathway as t e approaches zero. [ 1 ] Subcritical growth matters only if the lower threshold lies below the operating current. Lowack's initial numerical estimates put the two thresholds on a similar scale, while smaller grain-boundary formation energies could open a wider slow-growth regime. Preventing that slow failure would help where a critical-current-only picture might otherwise predict stability, not where it already predicts catastrophic fracture. [ 1 ] Interactive · Three ways to fail (or not) For fixed material and defect assumptions, the lower and upper onset thresholds stay fixed. Reducing electron leakage slows subcritical growth; it does not move the lower threshold in the stated equations. Plating current J (% of J_crit) 50% Electron transference t e … Regime … Failure time … Illustrative thresholds: Jsubcrit = 0.30 Jcrit is chosen for this diagram, not fitted. Jcrit is set to 50 mA/cm² for the time illustration. Failure time scales as 1/(te J), normalised to ten hours at te = 10⁻⁶ and J = 1 mA/cm². The actual subcritical threshold is uncertain. What the numerical discrepancy leaves open Using defects around 30 µm long and 50 nm wide with the sodium-electrolyte constants gives roughly 50 mA/cm², against a measured scale around 1 mA/cm². That factor-of-50 mismatch prevents treating the expression as a calibrated design limit. The paper discusses local toughness and grain-boundary effects as possible missing physics; those explanations still require independent measurements. [ 1 ] The sodium example draws on Anton and colleagues' tape-cast Na 5 RSi 4 O 12 work and related measurements cited by Lowack. It should not be attributed to a general reference on Weibull statistics. [ 3 ] The model suggests tests that can distinguish mechanisms: measure defect geometry, creep and local fracture resistance together; vary electronic leakage while keeping the mechanical interface comparable; and record failure times as well as a stepped-current threshold. Its useful contribution is a set of coupled dependencies and testable assumptions, with the absolute current scale still unresolved.

title: AI's Bottleneck Is Physical
summary: Sensing, data lineage, latency and safe interventions constrain industrial AI. A bottleneck illustration and deployment examples, rather than a fitted scaling law.
text: 19 July 2026 · AI & infrastructure AI's Bottleneck Is Physical Updated 11 November 2026 AI is often described in terms of models, parameters, tokens and prompts, but a deployed model lives inside a chain of physical transformations. Electricity becomes computation; computation becomes a decision; a decision becomes an action; an action changes a physical process; sensors observe the change. The next bottleneck in AI is not only better algorithms. It is whether this loop can be made reliable, efficient, and observable (and, if one can dream, even closed and self-improving). Trace one prediction A model is one component in a closed physical loop, not the loop itself. Select a stage to see the constraint that actually governs it. Interactive · The physical loop The loop is closed: sensor observations return as the next input, so a weakness at any stage limits the whole system, not just its own step. Deployment constraints Deployment depends on model quality, sensing, latency, energy, hardware integration and reliability. These variables have different units and interact differently. There is no fitted scaling law in this post. The widget below uses their minimum as a deliberately simple bottleneck score; it is not a multiplicative model or a measured performance predictor. A frontier model can be extraordinarily capable yet operationally useless for a millisecond-sensitive control loop, a disconnected production line, or a process whose sensors cannot identify the state that matters. Capability is not deployability Set model capability to 100% while keeping sensor quality or data context low. The deployable intelligence score stays low, because the system is a chain: the weakest interface, not the strongest component, sets what you can actually run. Industrial AI fails at interfaces, not just in neural networks. Interactive · Capability is not deployability … Illustrative bottleneck score Schematic. Drag any vertex to set that interface. The score is gated by the weakest one, so a single poor interface caps the system even at full model capability. The data centre becomes a factory Training has dominated the public imagination. While a training run is a discrete event, inference makes AI permanent infrastructure. A production model is a standing load that serves users, machines, or agents with predictable latency and availability. That requires power, networking, cooling, redundancy, and operational discipline. The International Energy Agency projects global data-centre electricity demand to increase from roughly 415 TWh in 2024 to about 945 TWh by 2030, driven substantially by AI-oriented accelerated computing. [IEA, 2025] For scale, the projected increase alone (about 530 TWh) is close to Germany's entire annual electricity consumption of roughly 500 TWh, and the 945 TWh 2030 total would rank among the largest national electricity demands on the planet (national comparisons are estimates). That electricity is not spent on one thing. In a typical facility the largest share powers the servers and accelerators doing the actual computation, much of the rest goes to cooling and power conversion, and within the compute portion the balance is shifting from training toward inference as models move into production. Cooling also has a second bill that rarely appears in FLOP counts: water. Evaporative and chilled-water systems consume large volumes of it, which turns selecting a location into a question of water availability as much as grid capacity, especially in dry regions and hot summers. Storage sits inside this picture. Data centres already use batteries for uninterrupted power and, increasingly, for buffering volatile loads, and distributed sensing and edge computing depend on them directly: wireless nodes, mobile inspection systems, robots, remote assets, and local backup. For a battery-powered sensor, communication, inference, and sampling become interchangeable energy expenditures, and the design question has no universal answer: is it cheaper to transmit raw data, extract features locally, infer locally, or transmit only an event? The important unit is therefore not only FLOPs. It is reliably delivered power. A model does not run on annual electricity statistics. It runs on megawatts, now, at a particular place on a particular grid. Germany: the industrial AI paradox Germany has an exceptional position in the application layer of AI: machinery, automation, precision sensors, industrial software, process engineering, electrochemistry, and manufacturing expertise. But it also exposes a simple tension: AI capacity cannot be deployed independently of power and grid infrastructure. Where does that stand today? German data centres were projected to consume 21.3 TWh of electricity in 2025, roughly 4% of the country's ~500 TWh annual demand. Installed capacity was expected to grow from nearly 3,000 MW to more than 5,000 MW by 2030, with AI-specific capacity projected to rise almost fourfold, from 530 MW to 2,020 MW. [Bitkom, 2025] The status quo is modest; the trajectory is steep, and it is concentrated in exactly the AI-specific, high-density load that is hardest to site. Connecting a high-density load requires grid capacity where fibre, cloud services, cooling options, industrial customers and skilled operators are available. Annual national generation says little about that local connection constraint. Sensors will close the AI loop The data centre is only one end of the AI system. At the other end, AI encounters the world through instruments. For an electrode-production line, the relevant observations might include material-lot identity, powder moisture, torque, temperature, pressure, roll speed, gap, thickness, mass loading, density, defect images, electrical resistance, and later electrochemical performance. There are crutches. Physics simulations, digital twins, and generative surrogates can, in theory, supply data where instrumentation is missing and even stand in for integration by producing labelled examples on demand. They are genuinely useful for pre-training and for exploring regimes that are expensive to measure. But a simulation is only ever as trustworthy as the physical assumptions inside it; at some point the loop still has to close against a real sensor, or the model is optimising a world that does not exist. Yet none of these observations is inherently a learning signal. A number becomes usable data only when it carries context: $$\text{measurement} + \text{identity} + \text{time} + \text{unit} + \text{process context} + \text{quality flag} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{evidence}$$ The factory, in the optimal case, produces measurements with intent and meaning. A bare temperature = 65 is not evidence until it carries its unit (65 °C, not 65 K), its location (drying zone 3, not ambient air), its time alignment (the correct electrode segment), its process state (recipe version 12, line speed 4 m/min), its provenance (sensor calibrated 18 days ago), and its quality flag (valid signal, no fault). Remove the timestamp alignment alone, and every analysis that links this reading to a specific electrode becomes invalid. Data harmonisation is the missing layer Most industrial AI efforts are not blocked by a lack of raw measurements. They are blocked because data cannot be reliably connected across the process. An electrode's eventual cell performance may depend on upstream material history, mixing, coating, drying, calendering, sampling location, cell assembly, formation protocol, and test conditions: $$\text{material lot} \to \text{mixing} \to \text{coated roll} \to \text{calendered sheet} \to \text{sample} \to \text{cell} \to \text{test}$$ If those records do not reference the same physical lineage, a model cannot learn process–property–performance relationships, no matter how sophisticated its architecture is. Break one identifier, shift one timestamp, or change one unit, and the graph forms false links: spurious correlations that a model will happily fit. Harmonisation is the interface between physical history and statistical learning. It is also where the causal question from my CausalPFN reading note becomes concrete: without lineage, you cannot even define the intervention whose effect you want to estimate. A sufficiently capable model could recover part of that structure on its own, probabilistic entity resolution to stitch fragmented lot and batch identifiers, learned alignment of asynchronous timestamps across logs, and causal-discovery constraints to reconstruct the process graph from weak signals, but each of these substitutes an inferred lineage for a recorded one, and inherits its uncertainty rather than removing it. Edge AI: compute where it matters The industrial answer is rarely "send every signal to the cloud." High-frequency camera streams, acoustic monitoring, and vibration signals can be costly to transfer and too delayed for a remote decision. Edge AI moves selected computation closer to the source: on a sensor, machine controller, local gateway, or factory server. Fraunhofer IPMS integrates signal processing and AI near sensors so that data can be processed where it is generated. [Fraunhofer IPMS, 2025] Computation belongs near the process when latency, bandwidth or resilience is decisive. Shared infrastructure is useful when fleet-wide context or larger models justify the communication cost. A practical design assigns each workload to a suitable level. Layer Typical function Appropriate intelligence Sensor Filtering, event detection, compression Rules, DSP, tiny neural network Machine Defect detection, anomaly scores, state estimation Compact vision or time-series model Factory Process coordination, multimodal prediction Site-level ML model Cloud Training, fleet learning, optimisation, simulation Large model or distributed compute Human Accountability, intervention, goal-setting Operator and engineer The allocation is a budget problem. More cloud processing adds global context but communication cost; more edge processing improves responsiveness but limits model capacity; more sensing improves observability but adds calibration and integration burden. There is no single optimum, only a trade-off surface. Detecting a problem is not the same as being able to fix it Whether an AI intervention is useful depends on more than the prediction. It depends on the actuators: their authority and precision, the process dead time before an action takes effect, the saturation limits that cap how far a setpoint can move, whether the transformation is reversible at all, and which variables can genuinely be manipulated rather than merely observed. In battery manufacturing this is decisive. Detecting a defect after coating or drying may already be too late to save that electrode: the material has passed through an irreversible step, and no downstream actuator can undo it. The useful question is therefore not "can the model detect the problem?" but "does the system detect it early enough, at a stage where an available actuator can still change the outcome?" A good predictor is not a good controller A highly accurate predictor can still produce poor control. It happens when measurements arrive late, when several controllers react to the same signal, when the model repeatedly overcorrects, when actuators respond more slowly than assumed, or when predictions are fed back as future inputs. The result is oscillation, overshoot, drifting setpoints, or competing optimisation loops that work against each other. Deployment therefore needs more than predictive validation. It needs shadow-mode testing, where the model runs alongside the process without acting; explicit stability margins; rate limits on how fast a setpoint may change; actuator constraints encoded into the policy; and a conservative fallback controller to hand back to when confidence drops. Causation needs intervention, and intervention must be safe Observational data can identify intervention effects under assumptions such as a valid causal graph, adequate overlap and control of relevant confounding. CausalPFN learns under a simulated family of such assumptions. Passive correlations alone do not guarantee that those conditions hold on a factory line. Deliberate interventions can resolve ambiguities, but they may produce scrap, damage equipment or require weeks of downstream testing. The experiment design must therefore include physical constraints and delayed outcomes. This is a safe-exploration problem: how does the system choose experiments that are informative without violating process constraints? The tools are known, constrained Bayesian optimisation, value-of-information scheduling, digital-twin screening followed by limited physical validation, and experiment designs that account for delayed downstream measurements, but each trades information against risk, and none removes the hard constraint that some regions of the process simply must not be entered. The model changes the world it learns from Once predictions influence operators or machine settings, the data stops being passive. The deployment policy changes which states are observed. Successful prevention makes certain failures disappear from the dataset entirely. Operator trust decides whether recommendations are followed at all. Optimisation can push the process into regions absent from the training data, and measured performance can become misleading precisely because the model altered the conditions under which it is judged. The model is no longer learning from a passive world; it is learning from a world partly created by its own previous decisions. That introduces feedback-selection bias and Goodhart-type effects, and it is why deployment needs policy-aware evaluation, counterfactual logging (recording what the model would have done alongside what was actually done), and carefully maintained control groups. It is the causal discipline from the harmonisation section again, now turned on the system's own actions. The edge case: failure Benchmarks assume stable inputs, stable hardware, and stable connectivity. Factories do not. A mature system needs to remain intelligible under sensor drift, network outages, version mismatches, power disturbances, and process changes. That means local buffering, explicit fallbacks, calibrated uncertainty, model-version tracking, and deterministic safety paths. Under a network loss or an edge-device failure, a fault-tolerant architecture routes around it: local inference continues, a rule-based fallback activates, data is buffered, or a human is alerted. A fragile architecture simply stops producing a decision. Reliability emerges from the architecture surrounding the model, not from the model alone. Closing the manufacturing loop For an electrode line, the useful evaluation combines accepted product, intervention time, energy use and failure recovery. Better sensors and data lineage make model errors easier to diagnose; local computation and bounded controllers determine whether a correction can arrive in time. These interfaces need to be measured together with predictive accuracy. For battery manufacturing, that is not a distant analogy. Batteries can power the distributed intelligence that improves battery production; manufacturing quality can determine the reliability of the storage supporting that intelligence. AI and advanced manufacturing are no longer separate sectors. Each increasingly defines the feasible scale, efficiency, and reliability of the other. title: Reading CausalPFN: Causal Effects as In-Context Prediction
summary: A NeurIPS 2025 paper trains one transformer on simulated, identifiable causal worlds; new observational data goes in as context, treatment-effect posteriors come out. What holds it up, and where it breaks.
text: 12 July 2026 · Reading notes Reading CausalPFN: Causal Effects as In-Context Prediction Updated 11 November 2026 Notes on Balazadeh, Kamkari, et al., CausalPFN: Amortized Causal Effect Estimation via In-Context Learning (NeurIPS 2025). Paper · Code Estimating a treatment effect from observational data usually starts with a choice: T-Learner or X-Learner, double machine learning or BART, a propensity model or an outcome model. Each fits some data-generating processes and fails on others, and telling which is which is expert work. CausalPFN asks whether that selection step can be trained away. Its answer is one transformer, trained once on a large library of simulated causal worlds, that reads a new observational dataset as context and returns effect estimates directly. No per-dataset fitting, no tuning. The idea transfers the prior-fitted network (PFN) recipe from tabular prediction to causal estimation. A PFN is trained on samples from a prior over data-generating processes (DGPs). At inference it approximates the posterior predictive distribution for a query, conditioned on the context set, in one forward pass. CausalPFN changes the target: instead of predicting the observable outcome, the network predicts the conditional expected potential outcome, the quantity that treatment effects are built from. The output is a quantized histogram over 1,024 bins, so each query returns a full distribution, not a point. The part I find most interesting: the prior does the causal work Nothing in the architecture is causal. The causal content sits entirely in the training distribution. Every simulated DGP draws covariates from real or synthetic base tables, relabels two columns as the potential outcomes, and assigns treatment by a random function of the covariates alone. Because treatment depends only on observed covariates, ignorability holds in every training world by construction. Proposition 1 states when this is enough. The posterior predictive converges to the true effect exactly when the prior is identifiable, meaning the effect is a functional of the observational distribution for almost every DGP the prior can generate. Identifiability is necessary and sufficient; the proof runs through Doob's classical consistency theorem. I read this as the paper's real thesis: amortized causal inference is possible to the extent that you can simulate worlds where the causal question has a unique answer. Interactive · Posterior concentration Grow the context: with an identifiable prior that covers the true DGP, the posterior for the effect narrows around the truth. Move the DGP outside the prior and the interval stays narrow but lands in the wrong place: confidently wrong. Validation-based temperature scaling can widen the interval; coverage outside the training prior is not guaranteed. Context size N 500 DGP outside the prior (OOD) Temperature calibration 90% interval width 0.31 True effect covered? Yes Schematic: the curves illustrate the behaviour described by Proposition 1 and Figure 7 of the paper (concentration under an identifiable prior; overconfidence out of distribution; temperature scaling can improve coverage on the evaluated distributions). They are not the trained model. Benchmark results and prior coverage On the standard benchmarks (100 IHDP realizations, 10 ACIC 2016 realizations, 200 Lalonde CPS/PSID realizations, 310 tasks in total), CausalPFN attains the best average rank for heterogeneous effects, 2.30 ± 0.10 against 3.57 for the next method, and the best mean PEHE on IHDP at 0.58 ± 0.07 (Table 1). It is also fast: inference is forward passes only, while the baselines pay for cross-validation and tuning on every new dataset (Figure 1). The comparison is honest about ATE, where CausalPFN's average rank of 4.45 sits slightly behind the plain T-Learner at 4.31. Two results temper the headline. On five large uplift-modeling RCTs, the model scores the best mean normalized Qini (0.952) on 50k-row subsamples, but performance drops when run on the full million-row tables; the authors attribute this to the context-length limits of PFN-style transformers. And calibration holds only in distribution: on DGPs outside the training prior the credible intervals become overconfident (Figure 7). The proposed fix is temperature scaling tuned on observational coverage, which improves calibration on the tested distributions. It cannot establish the absence of hidden confounders or guarantee calibration under every shift. The widget above mimics both failure and fix. Every training world satisfies ignorability , so the model answers every query as if treatment assignment were explainable by the observed covariates. Real observational data offers no such promise, and no amount of context tells the model that a confounder is missing. The same limitation applies to any estimator under ignorability; what changes here is that the assumption is baked into weights rather than stated per analysis. Why this matters for manufacturing data Process data from electrode manufacturing is observational in exactly the sense this paper targets. Nobody randomizes calendering pressure on a production line; settings correlate with material lots, operators, and everything else in the plant. Questions like "what did the pressure change do to capacity" are CATE questions asked of confounded data. An estimator that works out of the box, returns calibrated uncertainty, and needs no per-dataset tuning would lower the barrier considerably. The catch is the same as above: on a production line, the assumption that all confounders are recorded is rarely credible, and the model cannot flag its violation. Amortization is also where this touches my own work. A per-dataset estimator retrained after every process drift is exactly the setting where continual-learning questions appear. An in-context estimator sidesteps retraining: new data becomes new context. Whether that holds up under the drift patterns real plants produce is, to my reading, an open and testable question, and a cheaper one to test now that the model is public. title: The Geometry of Forgetting in Continual Learning
summary: An exact fixed-feature squared-loss calculation at stationarity, its second-order extension, and frozen-backbone IGFA results on Rotated-Digits.
text: 5 July 2026 · Continual learning The Geometry of Forgetting in Continual Learning Updated 11 November 2026, including preprint references published after the original post. Companion note to the draft Interference and retention in continual learning . Draft PDF When a network learns tasks in sequence it tends to suffer catastrophic forgetting : weights move to satisfy the new objective and, in doing so, dismantle the features that served the old one. The usual responses are engineering fixes. Experience replay retrains on stored samples; elastic regularisation penalises motion in directions the Fisher information marks as important. Both work. Neither says what forgetting is . For a linear readout with frozen features and squared loss, forgetting has a simple geometric form. Let Δ be an update away from a stationary point of Task A's objective. With the loss normalisation used here, its increase is exactly $$F(\Delta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \Delta^{\top} \Sigma_A\, \Delta$$ Here Σ A is the feature second-moment matrix, E[φφᵀ], or the covariance if features are centred. Squared loss makes this the constant Hessian. Without stationarity the loss change also contains ∇L A ᵀΔ, which can have either sign. In the stationary case, high-eigenvalue directions are expensive and an exact null-space direction leaves this objective unchanged. For a smooth nonlinear network, the local expansion is ΔL A = ∇L A ᵀΔ + ½ΔᵀH A Δ + o(‖Δ‖²). It is a second-order approximation; the linear term vanishes only at a stationary point. A frozen-feature model with cross-entropy is not globally quadratic either. Feature drift and larger updates need to be checked against the actual old-task loss. Interference-gated functional allocation (IGFA) IGFA uses the alignment between a proposed update and protected task directions to decide whether to share capacity or project the update. Below a threshold τ it leaves the update unchanged; above it, it removes the component in the protected subspace. This gives a concrete interference-control rule in the fixed-feature experiments, rather than a guarantee for an adapting deep encoder. There is no such thing as a free lunch: The projection discards part of the gradient. Task B learns more slowly, and in the limit of many protected tasks the free subspace shrinks toward nothing, creating a capacity ceiling. The gate is a hard threshold, so behaviour is discontinuous at τ. Whether that matters depends on how alignment is distributed in practice; on the sequences tested it does not, but that is an empirical claim about those sequences. Interactive · Vector alignment Rotate the proposed Task B update Δ B . Interference energy rises as it aligns with Task A's dominant direction. Above the gate threshold, IGFA projects the update onto the orthogonal complement. Shorter arrow > less progress > far less damage. Alignment angle θ 45° Cosine alignment 0.71 Interference, raw 52% Interference, after IGFA 2% Retained step length 71% IGFA gate (τ = 0.40) Projecting, Task A protected Model: Σ A = diag(1.00, 0.05), F(θ) = λ₁cos²θ + λ₂sin²θ, normalised to λ₁. The second eigenvalue is 0.05, so this example has no exact null space: even at θ = 90° a residual quadratic cost remains. Illustrative, not fitted to data. At θ = 0 the update lies straight along Task A's high-variance direction and interference is maximal. Rotating away, the raw interference falls as cos²θ, but the gate does not release until alignment drops below τ. In the gated region the projected update survives with length |Δ|·sinθ. So at θ = 20° the controller keeps roughly a third of the step, and near the threshold it keeps most of it. What the gate buys on a real benchmark The widget above is schematic. The figure below is not: it plots the measured accuracy–forgetting trade-off from the draft's Rotated-Digits benchmark (domain-incremental, five rotations, frozen backbone, mean ± 95% CI over five seeds). Measured, not schematic: Rotated-Digits domain-incremental results, mean ± 95% CI over five seeds (Table 2 of the draft). IGFA reaches the highest accuracy among replay- and Fisher-free methods (0.771 ± 0.030) with forgetting near zero (0.002 ± 0.027). Only replay scores higher (0.795 ± 0.012), and it pays for that with a stored data buffer. Next post Modelling the Electrode Calendering U-Shape

title: Modelling the Electrode Calendering U-Shape
summary: A process-dependent contact closure fits 27 graphite and NMC calendering states. Reorientation is a plausible graphite mechanism that thermal data alone cannot isolate.
text: 28 June 2026 · Electrode manufacturing Modelling the Electrode Calendering U-Shape Updated 11 November 2026, including preprint references published after the original post. Companion note to the preprint Capturing the calendering U-shape in lithium-ion electrode thermal conductivity . arXiv:2607.11521 · PDF Lithium-ion cells depend on calendered electrodes for volumetric energy density. Predicting what compression does to through-plane thermal conductivity (λ eff ) turns out to be harder than it looks. On first thought, a monotone relationship is expected: press harder, conductivity should rise. The measured conductivity can first fall and then recover during calendering. A porosity-only or static-contact closure misses that U-shape. Two plausible contributions are changing contact networks and, for graphite, particle reorientation. The thermal curve alone does not determine their individual shares. For quasi-isotropic NMC, a contact term that first weakens and then recovers can reproduce the U without a graphite-like orientation mechanism. Particle reorientation as a graphite hypothesis The missing mechanism is graphite anisotropy . Conductivity within the graphene planes is high; perpendicular to them it is poor, by more than an order of magnitude. Compression brings particles closer, but it also rotates them, laying the flakes flat against the current collector. Flat flakes present their poor through-plane axis to the direction heat must travel. Early calendering therefore trades a shrinking pore volume for a worsening particle orientation, if the orientation loss outweighs contact growth. Once most flakes are already aligned, further reorientation contributes less. At that point, growing particle-particle contact starts to dominate and the curve turns upward. The fitted closure adds a compression-dependent contact term φ(Π) to a Knudsen-corrected Zehner–Bauer–Schlünder base. Its in-sample MAPE falls from 31.1% to 4.5% over 27 states in four electrode families. A separate, bounded reorientation account is compared for graphite; it is not independently identified by this contact-term ablation. The 4.5% MAPE is in-sample across 27 states from four electrode families: thin and thick graphite anodes and thin and thick NMC cathodes. They come from one public dataset and one metrology chain. The draft reports 7.8% leave-one-state-out error. That checks interpolation within these families, while transfer to new recipes and measurement methods needs separate evidence. Table 3 compares M0, the zero-fit ZBS reference; M1, a fitted constant contact fraction; and M2, a process-dependent contact term φ(Π). This ablation measures the benefit of the contact model. It does not isolate reorientation, because M2 adds contact evolution rather than an independently measured texture contribution. Measured, not schematic: ablation MAPE from Table 3 of the draft. The constant contact fraction (M1) removes most of the offset (31.1% → 13.5% on average); the process-dependent φ(Π) term (M2) is what reproduces the U-shape and brings the average to 4.5%. Interactive · Calendering Compress the electrode. Particles flatten and rotate toward the horizontal; porosity falls monotonically. The dot tracks the calendering-aware prediction, which dips before it recovers (unlike the two monotone baselines). Compaction Π 0% Porosity ε 45.0% λ eff (through-plane) 0.60 W/mK Curves are schematic functional forms chosen to reproduce the qualitative behaviour of each closure, not the fitted model or the measured data. Read the shapes, not the values. A U-shaped response requires some contribution to turn downward or competing contributions to exchange dominance. It does not require both porosity and reorientation: a non-monotone contact network can be sufficient, as in the NMC fit. For graphite, same-sheet texture measurements alongside thermal and contact measurements would distinguish reorientation from contact damage and recovery. At VARTA and TU Braunschweig, my work spans hands-on electrode development , continual learning , and process–property modelling for changing materials and operating conditions. I work on this because reliable ML for battery manufacturing directly accelerates the transition to sustainable energy.
